articles.title: In 1980, a Louisiana drilling accident pierced a salt mine; within hours, Lake Peigneur became a whirlpool that swallowed a $5 million rig, barges, boats and trees
articles.summary: US News: On November 20, 1980, Lake Peigneur transformed from a shallow freshwater lake into a saltwater whirlpool due to a Texaco drilling accident that pierced an underground salt mine, causing catastrophic land erosion and swallowing multiple barges and a drilling rig.
articles.body: Lake Peigneur in southern Louisiana was a shallow freshwater lake on November 20, 1980, and by the time the disaster subsided, the lake had drained into an underground salt mine, a whirlpool had formed on its surface and the landscape around Jefferson Island had been altered. A Texaco drilling rig had accidentally penetrated the salt mine beneath the lake, and the resulting flow of water into the underground workings created a rapidly expanding crater that swallowed the rig, barges, a tugboat, trees and parts of the surrounding land. The Washington Post reported the following day that the $5 million drilling rig and other equipment had been pulled into the earth.The accident began when the drilling operation encountered the underground salt formation, when workers noticed problems with the rig and evacuated as the situation worsened. The Washington Post reported that seven men on the drilling rig and about 50 men in the salt mine escaped, and fortunately, no one was killed.The lake drained into the mineThe underground salt workings could no longer contain the flow as water rushed downward through the opening created by the drilling accident, and the water eroded the surrounding salt structure and enlarged the opening. The University of Louisiana at Lafayette’s Special Collections describes Lake Peigneur before the accident as a broad but extremely shallow lake of about 1,300 acres, with an average depth of only around 11 feet. The lake sat above the Diamond Crystal Salt mine, which made the underground workings an important part of what happened when the drilling operation breached the mine. The water formed a whirlpool that grew to roughly a quarter-mile across as the lake emptied, according to the university’s account. The current became powerful enough to reverse the flow of the nearby Delcambre Canal, which normally connected the lake with the Gulf of Mexico. Gulf water then rushed toward the newly created crater.Eleven barges, a tugboat, trees, sections of land and other structures were pulled toward the expanding hole. The Washington Post reported that the whirlpool also swallowed trees along the shoreline, and a federal mine-safety official warned that continued erosion could threaten the salt pillars supporting the island. Another danger was that the water entering the underground workings could weaken the salt columns supporting the mine. Workers escaped before the flooding became catastrophic, while those on the surface watched the lake disappear into the opening below.The lake did not return to its old stateLake Peigneur was no longer the same body of water once the flow slowed, and gulf water that was flowing backward through the canal refilled the depression. The University of Louisiana at Lafayette says that the lake eventually became roughly 200 feet deep and changed from freshwater to saltwater, and the nine barges that had been pulled under during the disaster later resurfaced. The university says that about 70 acres of land and trees were swallowed, along with parts of the botanical gardens on Jefferson Island. The lake had once been only about 11 feet deep, and now occupied a much deeper basin created by the collapse.A later Louisiana State University report on underground storage cites the 1980 accident as an example of the hazards associated with drilling into salt formations, and notes that the drilling rig accidentally punctured the top of the salt mine, after which water entered the mine and pulled 11 barges and surrounding land into the underground caverns. The report also records that the salt mine closed in 1986 and that the caverns were later used for natural-gas storage.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: We should use Reagan as a guide in handling our modern arms race with China
articles.summary: A former Air Force officer compares selling AI chips to China to giving nuclear technology to the Soviets, urging Trump to heed Reagan's Cold War lesson.
articles.body: I can still remember, as a young Air Force officer, sitting in the cockpit of my B-1 bomber knowing that we could deliver nuclear weapons virtually anywhere in the world. I also remember watching President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev meet in Reykjavik, Iceland, in 1986 to negotiate nuclear arms reductions. The whole world was watching. The nuclear arms race was a global threat, and the world’s two most powerful nations had a responsibility to confront it. Now imagine that, as Reagan sat across the table from Gorbachev, American companies were selling Moscow the technology it needed to make its nuclear arsenal even more powerful. ANTHROPIC CEO LIKENS AI FIGHT WITH CHINA TO COLD WAR, SEEKS 'DISARMAMENT NEGOTIATIONS' The idea would have been absurd. Yet today, as the United States enters another potentially historic technological arms race, we are entertaining a remarkably similar proposition: selling China the advanced computer chips it needs to build the world’s most powerful artificial intelligence. CHINA IS BUILDING AN AI WAR MACHINE. WASHINGTON MUST WAKE UP BEFORE IT’S TOO LATE Advanced AI chips are not nuclear weapons. But in the emerging competition over artificial intelligence, they may be the closest equivalent we have to the strategic materials that powered the last great arms race. In short, they are the fuel. Without enormous quantities of advanced chips and computing power, China cannot train frontier AI systems at the same scale or speed as the United States. That is precisely why Beijing wants them, and precisely why Washington should think very carefully before selling them. TRUMP'S AI RACE WITH CHINA COULD BECOME THE BIGGEST MISTAKE OF OUR TIME When President Donald Trump welcomes Chinese President Xi Jinping to the White House this month, there will be no shortage of issues to discuss. Trade. Security. Technology. The future of the world’s most consequential relationship. But Trump should make one principle clear: America will not help China build the technology that could erase one of our greatest strategic advantages. CHINA’S ROUTING OF BIDEN IN CHIP WAR WITH US CREATED A COMMUNIST TECH GIANT The United States currently possesses enormous leverage. America remains at the center of the world’s most advanced AI ecosystem, and China still depends heavily on access to American-designed chips and the broader technological infrastructure surrounding them. We should not give that leverage away. Earlier this year, the United States began allowing some advanced AI chips, including Nvidia’s H200, to be sold to China on a case-by-case basis. Those sales come with restrictions and security requirements. But the strategic question is more fundamental: Why should we accelerate China’s ability to compete with us in the first place? US ADVERSARY TURNS UP THE HEAT ON AMERICA’S AI LEAD WITH AN UNDERESTIMATED EDGE Supporters of chip sales argue that keeping China dependent on American technology preserves our influence and supports American companies. They also argue it disincentivizes China from developing its own capabilities. But there is great evidence that it has exactly the opposite effect. China is using our chips to accelerate their own capabilities. And national security should never be reduced to an argument over market share. Advanced AI chips are not nuclear weapons. But in the emerging competition over artificial intelligence, they may be the closest equivalent we have to the strategic materials that powered the last great arms race. In short, they are the fuel. An advanced AI chip sold to China does not simply power a search engine or make a factory more efficient. At sufficient scale, these chips provide the computing power required to train increasingly capable AI systems with applications in intelligence, cyber operations, military planning, autonomous weapons, scientific research and countless other fields. RUBIO WARNS AMERICA MUST 'STAY AHEAD OF THE CURVE' AS CHINA WORKS TO SURPASS THE US WITH STOLEN TECH We would never have looked at Soviet demand for strategic nuclear technology and concluded that the important question was whether an American company could make the sale. We understood that some technologies were too consequential to treat as ordinary commerce, and AI chips increasingly belong in that category. This does not mean America should retreat from AI development. Quite the opposite. We should build faster, innovate more aggressively and maintain as large a technological advantage over China as possible. But there is a difference between racing ahead and helping your adversary catch up. Trump should use the Xi meeting to turn America’s chip advantage into negotiating leverage. If China wants greater access to advanced American computing power, then Beijing should have to accept meaningful, verifiable limits on the most dangerous forms of AI development. We should demand transparency around massive compute clusters and clear restrictions on capabilities that could threaten U.S. national security or escape meaningful human control. And any agreement must be enforceable. China has given us little reason to rely on promises. The standard should be simple: Trust nothing. Verify everything. This is where Reagan’s example matters. He did not negotiate with the Soviet Union because America was weak. He rebuilt American strength first, then used that strength to secure limits on a dangerous arms race. He understood something we should remember today: You do not surrender your leverage before negotiations begin. Trump should apply that lesson to the defining technological competition of our time. America should lead in AI. America should win. And America should negotiate from strength to keep this race from carrying both nations somewhere neither can control. But we cannot negotiate from strength while handing China the fuel it needs to catch us. articles.title: 'A bit chubby': Memoir claims King Charles fat-shamed Diana; was 'giddily elated' by her death
articles.summary: UK News: Earl Spencer, brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, is set to release a memoir that makes a series of deeply personal claims about his sister’s relatio.
articles.body: Earl Spencer, brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, is set to release a memoir that makes a series of deeply personal claims about his sister’s relationship with King Charles, alleging that the then-Prince Charles sounded “giddily elated — like a lottery winner” when he called after Diana’s death in 1997 and that he once told her, shortly after their engagement, “Oh, a bit chubby here, aren’t we?”The allegations appear in Spencer’s forthcoming memoir titled ‘Swan Song: Diana, My Sister’, which is being serialised ahead of its publication. The book draws on Spencer’s recollections of his sister’s life, marriage and death nearly three decades ago.Buckingham Palace has already issued an unusually strong response to the book’s claims. While saying it does not comment on books as a matter of principle, a Palace spokesperson said King Charles was mindful that “the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory” even many years after a loss.‘Like a lottery winner’ after Diana’s deathSpencer writes that he was at his home in Cape Town with his children when he learnt that Diana had been killed in a car crash in Paris on August 31, 1997.After a series of calls confirming her death, Charles called Spencer, according to the memoir.Spencer claims that while other callers were stunned and struggled to express their condolences, Charles “sounded giddily elated — like a lottery winner”.He says Charles told him he had informed William and Harry of their mother’s death in their bedrooms at Balmoral. Spencer describes the conversation as “strangely matter-of-fact” given the circumstances.Looking back, Spencer says he suspects Charles may have been thinking about how Diana’s death could free him to marry the woman he loved, an interpretation that forms part of Spencer’s own recollection of the conversation.Charles fat-shames DianaAnother claim concerns Diana’s weight and eating disorder in the months before her wedding.Spencer writes that Diana was already struggling with an eating disorder when Charles allegedly squeezed her waist shortly after their engagement and remarked: “Oh, a bit chubby here, aren’t we?”He says the comment devastated Diana. According to Spencer, she later told him that her waist shrank from 29 inches to 23½ inches between her engagement and wedding.Spencer also claims that Diana had told a friend that Charles had confided to her on the eve of their wedding that he was happy to marry her but was not actually in love with her.‘We’ll forget her soon enough’Spencer recounts another alleged conversation with Charles during preparations for Diana’s funeral.He says he objected to William and Harry walking behind their mother’s coffin and subsequently received a call from Charles. Spencer describes Charles as becoming angry during the exchange.He claims that Charles eventually told him: “Rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough!”Spencer writes that he was so shocked by the remark that he told Charles he could not believe he had said it before ending the call.The Palace’s response came after this earlier extract was published. It did not directly address the individual allegations but questioned the reliability of memories shaped by grief decades after Diana’s death.The memoir also contains claims about Diana’s funeral arrangements, her decision to divorce Charles, her relationship with the royal household and her experiences during the breakdown of her marriage. Spencer says the book is intended, in part, to challenge what he considers “untruths” that emerged after his sister’s death.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Why the Kremlin fears even the ‘managed opposition’ in Russia
articles.summary: The risk of a protest vote was too high at the Duma elections so a pre-election crackdown was carried out.
articles.body:
In the weeks leading up to the Duma elections, the Kremlin accelerated what is known in the country as “ballot sterilisation”. It removed the remaining risk factors that could demonstrate any form of public dissatisfaction.

Candidates of the so-called managed opposition parties, such as the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (CPRF), have been arrested or barred from running, thus diminishing the prospect for a protest vote against the governing United Russia. Last month, Yabloko, the only openly antiwar party, was barred from fielding candidates.

In the past, voting for these parties has been encouraged by opposition leaders excluded from running, such as the late Kremlin critic Alexey Navalny , as a form of anti-regime vote.

This time the Kremlin is not taking any chances. Public dissatisfaction is widespread and the risk of a display of dissent at the ballot box is too high to let the managed opposition run freely. The election must produce a result that “proves” national unity and full support for President Vladimir Putin and the governing United Russia party.

Yabloko is the only surviving officially registered political party in Russia that adheres to democratic principles and openly opposes the war in Ukraine. It has pulled through multiple waves of political repression over the years that destroyed or forced all others into exile.

In July, Yabloko was allowed to register for the Duma elections. The decision to let the party run likely came out of the Kremlin’s desire to show confidence – to claim that elections in Russia are so free that even an openly antiwar party can participate amid the ongoing war with Ukraine.

Yabloko had about 4 percent support just before the election campaign started and was likely going to get between 1 and 2 percent of the vote, like in previous Duma elections – well below the 5 percent threshold to enter the legislature.

What changed? The registration of Yabloko prompted a mass, uncoordinated surge of interest due to its antiwar slogans. Searches in Russia’s top search engine, Yandex, containing the party’s name and the word “elections” increased fivefold , surpassing even those for the governing United Russia.

The explosion of interest in Yabloko was apparent across all popular social media platforms in Russia and was followed by statements of support and calls to vote for the party from exiled political leaders, such as Yulia Navalnaya, Navalny’s widow.

In August, the party’s registration for the election was revoked by the Supreme Court following accusations that it was seeking to undermine the electoral process.

The case of the CPRF is slightly different. It is the second-largest party in the Duma, and it votes on major bills “as requested” with United Russia. It is not openly antiwar, but it has multiple strong regional branches that tend to be more critical of the governing party at the local level, as well as a number of charismatic leading members who have been very vocal about the war’s negative consequences.

By building its campaign around targeted criticism, the CPRF has become a very attractive choice for protest voters.

The party has not been deregistered, but some of its candidates have been removed from the ballot under various pretexts, and a number of restrictions have been imposed that limit its campaigning.

For example, Nikolay Bondarenko, a popular communist with more than two million YouTube subscribers, was banned from participating in the Duma elections for the use of “extremist symbols”; the accusation is based on a social media post featuring Navalny’s photo.

Neither Yabloko nor CPRF would have threatened United Russia’s majority in the Duma if there had been no crackdown.

Years of perfected administrative pressure, investment in e-voting, the introduction of three-day voting, and the elimination of all independent election observers have made it extremely easy for the Kremlin to produce the outcome it desires.

The Kremlin’s political managers set the parameters for the election results in advance of the vote. Currently, the target is 50 percent turnout with 50 percent of the vote for United Russia. Notably, the latter was lowered from 55 to 50 percent due to concerns about growing public dissatisfaction.

So why the crackdown on the systemic opposition?

The elections are being held at a time when the direct consequences of the war in Ukraine are felt by a growing number of Russians. Fuel shortages and rising inflation are increasingly impacting Russian families, especially those who have not sent a member to the front or are working in the war industries.

People are growing more desperate and pessimistic about the future, especially in the more impoverished regions of the country. According to independent pollster Levada Center, public anxiety is at a level not seen since September 2022, when mass mobilisation was announced.

The Kremlin clearly perceives that there is a chance this dissatisfaction could pour out into the ballot boxes, which would necessitate more drastic measures of manipulation to adjust the result to the desired one.

If Yabloko, for example, were to get a double-digit result, this would be a nightmare for the Kremlin’s political managers. Even with all the tools for electoral manipulation at their disposal, it is impossible to make 10 percent into 1 percent without everyone knowing it.

This could elevate the risk of protests or substantially hurt the reputation of President Putin, who this year is personally promoting United Russia.

The results the Kremlin’s political managers must deliver need to demonstrate unity and full support – and those results need to be tacitly accepted by society at large.

The crackdown on the managed opposition, therefore, means that they have turned on overkill mode and are micromanaging every aspect of the electoral process.

The public mood would be a major concern for the Kremlin only until the elections are done. Once the vote has been conducted in a sufficiently satisfactory manner, the state apparatus will have a free hand to intensify political repression and adopt unpopular measures, such as total control over the internet or austerity policies.

The task of the Kremlin’s political managers, like that of the security agencies, is to maintain control no matter what, so that Putin can continue the war in Ukraine for as long as he needs to.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Iranians rally by the hundreds of thousands in biggest show of defiance since war began
articles.summary: Hundreds of thousands of Iranians rallied Friday in a government-organized show of defiance after months of war, pledging their readiness to take up arms in the biggest such demonstration since the United States and Israel attacked in February.
articles.body: Hundreds of thousands of Iranians rallied Friday in a government-organized show of defiance after months of war, pledging their readiness to take up arms in the biggest such demonstration since the United States and Israel attacked in February. Iran’s government has sought to rally the people and stress national unity, even as the economy worsens under a U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports and new U.S. sanctions meant to increase Tehran’s economic pain. Estimates varied of the number of people volunteering to receive limited military training and defend the country in an effort described as “Janfaday-e Iran,” or the “ones who sacrifice their lives for Iran.” They marched through downtown Tehran in combat uniform, carrying flags, as onlookers cheered. For days, state media have encouraged Iranians to join the campaign, saying training with assault rifles would begin soon. The volunteers would be an additional layer of security to the powerful Revolutionary Guard paramilitary and its all-volunteer arm, the Basij. Tehran’s Guard chief, Gen. Hassan Hassanzadeh, told the state broadcaster that over 600,000 people had registered to participate, with over 1 million expected to take part in the training. On Friday morning, the broadcaster estimated over 300,000 people were on the streets. The new head of the Basij, Hossein Taeb, declared in a speech as the rally began that the volunteers will be ready for “full-fledged defense” and similar rallies will take place in other cities soon. The new trainees will make a “nightmare” for Iran’s enemies, Taeb added, as President Masoud Pezeshkian, military commanders and other senior officials watched the march. Some participants trampled flags of the U.S. and Israel. Others chanted “Death to America” and “Death to Israel.” “I am here to tell (President Donald) Trump that we Iranians have no fear about his threats against our homeland,” said Marzieh Afaghi, 24, who attended the rally with her toddler and husband. “No one in history could invade Iran and remain there.” The rally was also a chance for Iran to show off military hardware. Anti-aircraft batteries were on display, while female Guard members in black headscarves sat with truck-mounted machine guns. The Guard displayed drones that have been widely used against ships in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has asserted control since the war began, severely affecting the Gulf region’s shipments of oil and natural gas to the rest of the world. Friday’s events also suggested that hardliners like Taeb among Iran’s leadership will be more prepared to suppress any future demonstration against the theocracy. In January, shortly before the war, Iran saw some of its largest nationwide protests in history, which began over the struggling economy and turned to wider grievances. Activists have said a crackdown killed over 7,000 people and saw tens of thousands detained. In May, government officials said more than 30 million people in Iran — home to a population of some 90 million — had volunteered via an online form or at public gatherings to lay down their lives for the theocracy. The Associated Press could not independently confirm that.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) co-convener Ashutosh Ranka on Friday questioned a private news channel's decision to honour Jaipur's Neerja Modi School with an award, citing the death of nine-year-old student Amaira and subsequent action taken by the CBSE against the school.The school received the "Excellence in Developing Young Leaders and Changemakers" award at a ceremony held in New Delhi on September 16.Calling the decision "shocking", Ranka questioned whether the organisers were aware of the circumstances surrounding Amaira's death. Are you aware that the first thing the school did after the incident was to wipe off the floor? Are you aware that the school's affiliation from Class 9-12 was cancelled by the CBSE for gross safety violations?" he asked in a social media post."If yes and you still decided to award the school, you are also a perpetrator of injustice like so many others," he said.Police have filed a chargesheet in connection with Amaira's death.(With Agency Inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Psychosis evidence changes everything in Clancy judge's other killer mom case: retired judge
articles.summary: Judge William Sullivan, who declared a mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy case, also presided over the Latarsha Sanders trial now vacated by the court.
articles.body: Judge William Sullivan, who drew national attention earlier this month after declaring a mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy murder case, also presided over another closely watched child-killing trial that a retired Massachusetts judge says would look dramatically different if retried. The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court last month vacated the murder conviction of Brockton mother Latarsha Sanders, ruling jurors were improperly prevented from seeing psychiatric records central to her insanity defense and ordering a new trial. "They ordered a new trial which will fundamentally change the way the case is going to be tried," retired Massachusetts Superior Court Judge Jack Lu told Fox News Digital. LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL DECLARED AFTER JURY DEADLOCKS IN KILLINGS OF HER THREE CHILDREN Sullivan, who presided over Sanders' 2022 trial and later sentenced her to two concurrent life terms without parole, has returned to the national spotlight following the closely watched Clancy trial, which ended in a mistrial after jurors deadlocked over whether Clancy was criminally responsible for killing her three children. Like Sanders, Clancy admitted killing her children but argued she lacked criminal responsibility because of mental illness. "There is no doubt the defendant committed these incomprehensible crimes," Justice David Gaziano wrote for the unanimous court in Sanders' case. "The sole issue before a Superior Court jury was whether she lacked criminal responsibility." LINDSAY CLANCY JUDGE CALLS MISTRIAL, THEN GRANTS DEFENSE ONE HOUR STAY FOR APPEAL The justices concluded Sanders was entitled to a new trial because jurors never saw medical records documenting diagnoses and treatment of mental illness that were relevant to the only issue disputed at trial: whether she lacked criminal responsibility. Lu said the ruling does far more than simply order another trial. "Thousands of pages of mental health records will be admitted ... and the jury's gonna get it all," he said. Lu cautioned against judging Sullivan's decision with the benefit of hindsight. "The trial judge did an excellent job ... but now I'm a great Monday morning quarterback just like everybody else," Lu said, explaining that the evidentiary issue was unusually difficult before the SJC clarified the law. Sanders admitted killing her sons, 8-year-old Edson "Marlon" Brito and 5-year-old La'Son Brito, but argued she was legally insane at the time of the attacks. Her attorneys contended she was suffering from severe mental illness and psychosis, while prosecutors argued she appreciated the wrongfulness of her actions despite bizarre statements she made before and after the killings. According to evidence summarized by the Supreme Judicial Court, Sanders had become consumed by conspiracy theories involving the Illuminati and expressed fears about voodoo before the killings. After the deaths, investigators said she gave police multiple conflicting accounts before eventually telling detectives the stabbings were part of a "ritual" tied to voodoo and the Illuminati. At trial, Sanders' defense called a clinical neuropsychologist who testified she was "grossly psychotic" at the time of the killings and suffered from a schizophrenia-spectrum disorder. The expert based that opinion in part on thousands of pages of psychiatric treatment records from prison and a state psychiatric hospital. Those are the records Lu said a future jury would likely hear if prosecutors pursue another trial. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X The Supreme Judicial Court said that was an error, concluding the excluded records documented repeated observations of paranoia, hallucinations, delusional thinking and schizophrenia-spectrum diagnoses that formed the medical foundation of Sanders' defense. Read the court's ruling: "We hold that the exclusion of the MCI-Framingham and WRCH medical records documenting the defendant's post-arrest diagnoses or treatment of mental illness ... impermissibly stripped the sole defense 'of the medical foundation that supported it,'" the court wrote. "The defendant is entitled to a new trial." SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS Lu said the opinion should not be interpreted as a determination that Sanders was legally insane or wrongly convicted. Instead, he described it as the resolution of a difficult evidentiary question that changes what evidence jurors would be permitted to consider if the case is retried. During oral arguments before the Supreme Judicial Court, Sanders' attorney, Robert Shaw, argued the trial judge's exclusion of medical evidence deprived his client of "a meaningful opportunity to present a complete defense," FOX 25 in Boston reported. CLICK HERE FOR MORE Assistant Plymouth County District Attorney Melissa Johnson countered that Sanders showed no documented psychotic behavior for months after the killings and that the records were properly excluded, the station reported. SEND US A TIP The justices also addressed two issues that would likely shape any future trial. GOT A TIP? First, they said prosecutors could refer to Sanders describing herself as "evil" because the statements were relevant to whether she appreciated the moral wrongfulness of her actions, so long as the argument remained tied to that legal issue rather than serving as a personal attack. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST However, the court found prosecutors improperly suggested Sanders may have borrowed elements of her story from episodes of "Law & Order: SVU," ruling there was no evidence supporting that theory. GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL The ruling vacates Sanders' convictions and sends the case back to Plymouth Superior Court for a new trial. An overturned conviction does not clear Sanders of the charges, Lu said. "It just means you have to do it all over again," he said. articles.title: Man loses weight eating nothing but a certain food for 25 days — and paid a price
articles.summary: A New Jersey man's Sweetgreen-only diet for 25 days left him nine pounds lighter — but the cost, logistics and a celebratory cheese pizza tell a bigger story.
articles.body: A New Jersey man ate nothing but certain foods from a fast-casual chain for 25 days — an experiment that left him nine pounds lighter and craving a slice of pizza. Tim Donahue, a 27-year-old Hoboken resident who works in advertising in New York City, documented his challenge as a modern-day spin on Morgan Spurlock's 2004 documentary "Super Size Me," he told Fox News Digital. But instead of eating McDonald's for a month, Donahue wanted to see what would happen if he exclusively ate at a chain on the opposite end of the fast-food spectrum. AMERICA'S FAVORITE FAST-FOOD CHAIN NAMED: MCDONALD'S WINS HEARTS BUT NOT BEST BURGER, SURVEY SAYS "I think it felt the furthest possible opposite of McDonald's," Donahue said of choosing Sweetgreen. The idea also came from watching his health-conscious co-workers routinely order Sweetgreen for lunch while he showed up with fast food. "Everyone inside my office is very healthy, and they were getting Sweetgreen bowls every single day for lunch," Donahue said. "I myself would go pick up a fast-food burger and everyone would razz and make fun of me." Donahue originally intended to make his experiment last for 30 days, but there was a practical problem. EATING 5 FRUITS AND VEGETABLES A DAY MAY NOT BE ENOUGH FOR HEART HEALTH, STUDY FINDS "I wanted to do 30, but if you try to look at your calendar and try to fit [it into] any 30-day window, there was always a wedding, a work trip, a reason why I couldn't do 30," he said. "I said, 'You know what, it's either going to get done with 25 days or I'm never going to it done.'" His primary rule was simple: Whatever he consumed had to be available on Sweetgreen's menu, although he made an exception for black coffee. And while Sweetgreen offers more than salads, Donahue tried to keep the experiment centered on its bowls. By the third day, he said, there was little chance of turning back. 9 pounds down as a favorite emerges Donahue didn't begin the challenge expecting to lose weight, but by the end, the number on his scale had dropped by about nine pounds. He also found a clear favorite on the menu. AMERICA'S LATE-NIGHT FAST-FOOD CULTURE MAY BE MAKING A COMEBACK — HERE'S WHY "I was rocking with the hot honey chicken bowl," he said. "I was getting that all the time." Donahue said the variety made eating from the same restaurant for nearly a month easier than one might expect. The bigger challenge, he said, was arranging his life around the experiment. "The most challenging aspect of the project was not the food, it was the logistics," he said. Meals had to be planned around the store's operating hours. Going out with friends meant skipping drinks and potentially bringing a salad along. Even dates with his girlfriend took a back seat. 'Not a sustainable thing' One thing Donahue doesn't recommend about his experiment today is the price tag. "You can cook at home and make a salad at home and spend a significantly smaller amount of money," he said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Donahue said he offset some of the expense by deciding not to spend money on alcohol or other restaurant meals during the challenge. But, he admitted, it was a "very expensive" project. "Out of pocket, this is not a sustainable thing to do over groceries," he said. Donahue also emphasized that Sweetgreen didn't pay him to conduct the experiment. The company subsequently embraced his idea, Donahue said. "His video inspired us to launch our own 30-day Sweetgreen challenge," Nicolas Jammet, Sweetgreen's co-founder and chief concept officer, told Fox News Digital. "We put out an open call for 30 participants to eat only Sweetgreen for 30 days and document how they feel throughout, and we already received hundreds of applications." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS After 25 days of salad bowls, Donahue headed to his favorite neighborhood pizzeria. "A cheese pizza after a month of salads was incredibly well-deserved," he said. There was just one problem. The sudden return to heavier food didn't sit particularly well. "It did make me feel quite sick because it's a shock to your system," Donahue said. articles.title: Top DOJ official warns of deadly smuggling route after 42 vanish at sea
articles.summary: The Justice Department says 42 people vanished at sea after a Colombian smuggler guided them onto a boat from San Andrés Island to Nicaragua.
articles.body: A Colombian smuggler’s guilty plea is shedding new light on a deadly route to the United States after a boat carrying 42 people vanished at sea and a top Justice Department official said the danger would not have ended if they reached land. Luis Enrique Linero Pinto, 41, also known as "El Calvo," pleaded guilty in federal court in El Paso, Texas, after being extradited from Colombia for his role in a smuggling conspiracy that prosecutors said used bribery and maritime routes to move migrants north. The boat left Colombia’s San Andrés Island for Nicaragua on Oct. 21, 2023, carrying approximately 40 migrants and two captains. It never arrived, and no one aboard has been seen or heard from since. "This was a particularly sad and disturbing situation," Assistant Attorney General Tysen Duva, who leads the Justice Department’s Criminal Division, told Fox News Digital. OVERCROWDED MIGRANT VESSEL WITH 240 PEOPLE ON BOARD INTERCEPTED NEAR TURKS AND CAICOS "These 40 individuals and the two boat captains, once they set out from San Andrés Island to Nicaragua, were never heard from again," Duva said. "These individuals are, of course, missing and presumed dead, and it appears that there were no survivors." ELEVEN INDICTED IN ALLEGED TEXAS SMUGGLING SCHEME THAT LEFT 7 MIGRANTS DEAD IN SHIPPING CONTAINER Duva said the disappearance offers a brutal look at the danger posed by transnational smuggling organizations that turn vulnerable migrants into commodities while pursuing routes toward the United States. "It’s all about money," he said. "Anybody who’s involved with a cartel or transnational smuggling in this regard, it is about money. It’s about preying on people’s misfortune." MEXICAN NATIONAL SENTENCED IN BORDER CHILD SMUGGLING CASE INVOLVING THC-LACED CANDY According to the Justice Department, Linero Pinto advised migrants on how to reach San Andrés Island, personally received them upon arrival, arranged their accommodations and transported them to boats bound for Nicaragua. From there, the migrants intended to travel through Central America and Mexico before illegally entering the United States, prosecutors said. CBP JOINS FORCES WITH COAST GUARD TO INTERCEPT 3 SMUGGLING BOATS, APPREHEND 60 PEOPLE OFF CALIFORNIA COAST Linero Pinto also bribed members of the Colombian navy to obtain real-time intelligence about the positions of patrol vessels between San Andrés Island and Nicaragua, allowing smuggling boats to evade authorities, according to court documents. He admitted helping smuggle the migrants aboard the boat that vanished in October 2023. INSIDE UNDERGROUND EL PASO STORM DRAIN SYSTEM BORDER PATROL SAYS CARTELS EXPLOIT TO SMUGGLE ILLEGAL MIGRANTS Duva said the victims had not even completed the opening stretch of the dangerous route when they disappeared. "That’s the first leg. They didn’t even finish the first leg here and get to Nicaragua and then try to come north by land," he said. "It’s a really long journey, and it’s full of really bad things that can happen." DOJ SAYS 11 MIGRANTS INDICTED IN MULTI-STATE SEX TRAFFICKING, DRUG, FIREARMS CASE The danger, he warned, is not confined to the open water. Duva said migrants can face treacherous terrain while traveling through South and Central America and across the U.S.-Mexico border. Even those who reach the United States may be trapped by mounting debts and pushed into sex trafficking, he warned. "You pay money to come to the United States, and then when you get here, the co-conspirators or those involved in the criminal enterprise will say, ‘But now you owe more, and you’re going to work this off in the sex trade,’" Duva said. "Cross-border smuggling cases often times just morph right into human trafficking cases," he continued. "The crime sort of changes along the way. The travelers are the ones victimized, and this comes at a significant cost in terms of public safety." Linero Pinto was charged in October 2024 and arrested in Colombia that December at the request of the U.S. government. He was later extradited to the United States and made his first appearance in federal court in El Paso in December 2025. He pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit alien smuggling and placing lives in jeopardy. He faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison, though a sentencing date has not been set. ‘GHOSTS’ ON FLORIDA HIGHWAYS: ROADSIDE STINGS SNARE 249 ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS, OFFICERS WARN MANY MORE HIDING A case against alleged co-conspirator Hernando Manuel de la Cruz Rivera Orjuela remains pending, Duva said. The prosecution is part of Operation Take Back America and was coordinated by Joint Task Force Alpha, the Justice Department-led initiative targeting cartels and other transnational organizations involved in high-impact human smuggling and trafficking. Duva praised President Donald Trump and his administration for putting a "tremendous focus" on the initiative and providing the Justice Department with additional resources to pursue smugglers, cartels and other transnational criminal organizations. "We’re super thankful to President Trump," Duva said. "We’re deeply thankful to the White House for that. We’re thankful to Congress for that, and we’re going to keep doing what we’re doing." Duva said funding approved through Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill allowed the Criminal Division to hire additional prosecutors and place experienced attorneys in sections handling the administration’s priorities. "People think, ‘Well, what is that? What did it do?’" he said. "We’re feeling the effects of that. We’re able to put skilled prosecutors in these different sections to attack these administration priorities." Duva said the task force is hunting criminal networks along the southern border, maritime routes near Florida and the northern border with Canada. "We are focusing on these cases at any border that we have," he said. His warning to smugglers operating beyond America’s borders was blunt. "Our reach is substantial," Duva said. "We are going to chase these cases no matter where they originate from or where we find them." Duva said the department’s expanded international partnerships are critical because the criminals behind the operations often believe distance will protect them from prosecution. "They just think, ‘Well, they catch other people, but they’re not going to get me,’" he said. "You really try to combat that one case at a time." Joint Task Force Alpha has produced more than 483 domestic and international arrests, over 436 U.S. convictions and more than 371 significant prison sentences, according to the Justice Department. FIRST TREN DE ARAGUA GANG MEMBER EXTRADITED TO US ON HISTORIC TERRORISM CHARGES APPEARS BEFORE HOUSTON JUDGE Duva said the mission should transcend partisan fights because the networks being targeted threaten migrants and American communities alike. "It shouldn’t be partisan," he said. "It should be obvious that anybody who’s in the White House, anybody who is in Congress, should be lauding these cases and the work that’s being done by Criminal Division entities like Joint Task Force Alpha." The Justice Department’s ultimate goal, Duva said, is the "total elimination" of cartels and the criminal organizations profiting from human suffering. "You do it one case at a time," he said. "We are focused on doing the very best cases that we can for the American people. That’s what we get up every day and think about." For Duva, however, the vanished boat remains a haunting illustration of why that mission matters. "It’s super tragic, and hopefully people realize when they hear about this case just how dangerous it is and how important it is that you target these smuggling groups."

articles.title: In 1998, Peninsular bighorn sheep were listed as endangered in California’s desert mountains; the introduced aoudad later raised competition concerns in similar arid habitats
articles.summary: US News: Explore the ecological implications of aoudad sheep introduced to California's Santa Rosa Mountains and their competition with endangered desert bighorn sheep for resources.
articles.body: Aoudad, also known as Barbary sheep, are native to the mountains and deserts of northern Africa, but were introduced to parts of the American Southwest as exotic game animals. Their ability to survive in dry, rugged terrain eventually brought them into contact with native species that depend on many of the same resources.According to the National Park Service, aoudad were introduced into the Southwest for hunting and subsequently established wild populations. In desert environments, their ability to tolerate heat, use rugged terrain and feed on a wide range of plants has allowed them to persist. In California, this matters because the same type of steep, arid country is occupied by desert bighorn sheep, including the protected Peninsular population of the Santa Rosa Mountains.From game animal to established populationThe introduction of aoudad to the American Southwest came through intentional releases. Wildlife managers introduced the animals in different areas because of their size, distinctive horns and hardiness in harsh conditions. However, once introduced, the aoudad became less reliant on management by humans. Their adaptability allowed them to establish themselves in landscapes that many large mammals struggled to inhabit.That adaptability is particularly important in desert ecosystems. The National Park Service describes aoudad as an introduced species that has become established in several parts of the Southwest, while noting that they can occupy habitat once used by native bighorn sheep. The history shows how an introduction made for hunting can later become a wildlife-management problem. California's Santa Rosa Mountains provide an important example of the habitat at stake. The California Department of Fish and Wildlife says the Santa Rosa Wildlife Area covers about 101,500 acres and contains the largest herd of protected Peninsular bighorn sheep in the United States.When two sheep use the same desertThe issue stems from how similar the two species are. Both aoudads and desert bighorn sheep have adapted to living in mountainous and rocky areas in arid climates. Both species also rely on vegetation and water resources that are especially limited at certain times of year. The California Department of Fish and Wildlife further adds that Peninsular bighorn sheep inhabit a small geographical area at the base of the Peninsular Ranges. The distribution of this type of animal is influenced by such factors as topography, visibility, water sources, and the amount of forage available. Canyon bottoms, washes, and alluvial fans become particularly important since they provide water and forage sources.Research published in the Journal of Wildlife Management provides a closer look at what happens when the two species share the same landscape. Scientists analysed the diets of aoudad and desert bighorn sheep in the Sierra Vieja Mountains of West Texas using DNA metabarcoding of faecal samples. They identified 88 plant genera consumed by the two species. The diets were more similar during the warm-dry season, when forage was more limited, suggesting that periods of resource scarcity could increase the potential for competition. There was another important difference in their diets. Whereas bighorn sheep preferred higher-quality forage, aoudads had a more general diet and could use lower-quality food sources more efficiently. This finding does not prove that aoudad are displacing bighorns in California, but it helps explain why competition between the two species is a concern.A longer conservation challengeCompetition with yet another herbivore is only one part of a broader conservation challenge for desert bighorn sheep. Desert bighorn sheep inhabit naturally limited regions, and the presence of water and suitable grazing areas determines the location and size of each herd. According to the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, the Peninsular bighorn sheep exist in geographically isolated herds from the San Jacinto Mountains all the way down to the Mexico-California border. Migration between herds is important for reaching resources and maintaining genetic links between them.Environmental factors affect the animals in their natural habitat as well. According to CDFW, lamb survival may vary significantly among populations and seasons and may be affected by rain that influences the productivity of vegetation and diseases. The monitoring includes ground surveys and satellite and VHF collar tracking for the purpose of studying the movement patterns of the animals. Thus, the aoudad story goes beyond the species’ initial introduction as a game animal. It raises the question of how an introduced sheep species fits into an ecosystem that already has a native one, especially when wildlife managers are trying to conserve scarce resources for both.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Bomb attack at Pakistan mosque kills at least 16 people, injures 56
articles.summary: Attack not immediately claimed, but ISIL and Pakistan Taliban (TTP) active in the region and regularly target troops.
articles.body:
A bomb attack at a mosque and subsequent gun battle in Pakistan’s restive northwest has killed at least 16 people, including five police officers, with more than 56 reported injured.

An explosive-laden car was rammed into the entrance of a mosque located at a police headquarters in Kohat, in the province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa near the Afghan border, as people gathered for Friday prayers.

There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack. However, both a regional affiliate of the ISIL (ISIS) armed group and the Pakistan Taliban (TTP) are active in the region and regularly target security forces.

Provincial police chief Zulfikar Hameed confirmed that the bombing had been a suicide attack. After the explosion, gunmen attempted to enter the police compound and exchanged fire with officers.

At least 15 bodies and more than 50 injured were initially taken to hospital, said Dr Tahir Shah, according to the dpa news agency. The death toll could rise as several injured people were in critical condition, he added.

Hospital officials have confirmed that five police officers and 10 civilians were among the dead, Bilal Faizi, a senior rescue official, said, according to the AP news agency. Most of those wounded were worshippers.

The mosque was badly damaged and the police station’s outer wall collapsed. Residents said the blast had been heard some distance away.

Most suspicion over the attack is likely to fall on the TTP. It came a day after a roadside bomb struck a security forces convoy in the northwestern Hangu district and killed six soldiers.

Government troops conducted raids in various areas on Thursday and killed 10 fighters believed to be members of the TTP, the military and police said.

The group is separate from, but allied with, the Taliban, which returned to power in Afghanistan in 2021.

Violence has surged in Pakistan’s remote regions near the Afghan border since, and Islamabad accuses the Taliban of allowing the groups that orchestrate attacks to operate from Afghan territory.

Officials in Kabul deny the accusation. The tension has seen the two nations launch cross-border attacks on an intermittent basis.

Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the bomb attack and directed authorities to accelerate rescue operations.

The Ministry of Interior said the “cowardly actions” of the attackers could not weaken the “nation’s firm resolve”.

articles.title: US national VanDyke gets default bail in NIA terror conspiracy case
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The Rouse Avenue Court in Delhi has granted default bail to US national Matthew Aaron VanDyke in a case registered by the National Investig.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Rouse Avenue Court in Delhi has granted default bail to US national Matthew Aaron VanDyke in a case registered by the National Investigation Agency (NIA).The court granted bail to VanDyke on a personal bond of Rs one lakh and one surety of the like amount, and directed him to stay in Delhi. It also directed him to remain available for investigation whenever called by the Investigation Officer.The court observed that the six Ukrainian nationals accused in the case also have a right to bail if they file bail applications.The NIA has filed a charge sheet against all seven foreigners without invoking sections of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA).VanDyke and Ukrainian nationals Kaminskyi Viktor, Hurba Petro, Slyviak Taras, Ivan Sukmanovskyi, Stefankiv Marian and Honcharuk Maksim were arrested in March for allegedly travelling to Mizoram without the required permits and crossing into Myanmar.An FIR was registered against them. The NIA has said that its investigation into the matter is ongoing and that it may file a supplementary charge sheet if an offence under the UAPA is established, the agency's Special Public Prosecutor (SPP) told the court, as cited by ANI.The agency has invoked Sections 21 and 23 of the Immigration and Foreigners Act against the accused. Counsel for the accused had submitted that these are compoundable offences at the level of the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO).The court has listed the charge sheet for consideration on October 1. The accused were arrested in a case concerning the alleged training of ethnic armed groups in Myanmar that were inimical to India's national security and remained in custody for around 180 days after their arrest in May 2026.In its charge sheet, the NIA accused the seven of offences under Sections 21 and 23 of the Immigration and Foreigners Act and said, "more time is required to ascertain and verify the true and complete facts about the commission of offences under UAPA."Following their arrest, the NIA had told the court that the accused were being investigated as part of a wider terror conspiracy, including allegedly assisting ethnic armed groups in India and Myanmar and imparting drone training to them.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘My children did not attack Iran’: 2bn South Asians suffer from distant war
articles.summary: A quarter of the world’s population faces a surging cost of living crisis because of the wars in the Middle East.
articles.body:
India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Nepal are together home to nearly two billion people, about 23 percent of the world’s population. Even before the war on Iran, the region depended heavily on imported energy, much of it from Gulf countries.

But the extent and nature of exposure of different South Asian countries to Gulf supplies and the Strait of Hormuz varied significantly.

Now, they are all feeling the effects of the prolonged and expanding war, as more and more supply routes become choked.

India imports about 85 percent of the crude oil it consumes – it is the world’s third-largest crude importer.

Before the war, Gulf producers, including Iraq, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Kuwait, were among its major suppliers, while Qatar was a leading source of liquefied natural gas (LNG). India has a more diversified supply network than its South Asian neighbours, with crude also arriving from Russia, Africa and the Americas.

Pakistan is also highly dependent on imported energy, particularly crude oil, petroleum products and LNG. Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Kuwait have traditionally been important oil suppliers, while Qatar is its main long-term LNG provider.

Bangladesh produces natural gas domestically, but increasingly relies on imported LNG as local production struggles to meet demand.

Qatar is one of its main LNG suppliers, while the country also imports refined petroleum products.

Nepal has no direct crude oil or LNG imports from the Gulf. Instead, the landlocked country relies on India for virtually all of its petroleum products, including petrol, diesel, kerosene and LPG. Its exposure to Gulf disruptions is indirect: higher costs or supply shortages in India can feed through to Nepal’s fuel supplies and prices.

India faces the largest exposure in absolute volumes, while Pakistan and Bangladesh have fewer alternatives for some critical energy supplies. Nepal’s dependence is one step removed, but disruptions to India’s energy supply chain can quickly reach the Nepali market.

As is often the case, it is the poor and economically vulnerable who are bearing the brunt of the crisis.

‘Financially, I feel completely helpless’

Sajida Jibran is a 45-year-old housekeeper in Pakistan’s southern coastal city of Karachi.

She works long hours in an affluent neighbourhood, has a husband who can no longer work due to health issues and she has three children in middle and high school.

Jibran says her rent has gone up from 15,000 Pakistani rupees ($54) at the end of last year to 25,000 rupees ( 90) this past month.

“Before the war, everyone could eat and drink. I could buy meat, chicken, but since the war started, even vegetables have become so expensive that it is difficult to buy them,” she said.

“The price of electricity has increased a lot, our bill used to come to around 1,500 [rupees] ($5.4), but now it starts at 5,000 ($18). The gas bill is also very high and comes to a minimum of 2,000 rupees ($7),” said Jibran. Natural gas bills in Pakistan have historically been minimal because it was locally produced, but having depleted its reserves, Pakistan largely imports natural gas.

The hardest decision Jibran has had to make was to stop paying her children’s school fees: she could either educate them or feed them.

“I had always hoped that my children would study, get a good education and have the opportunity to attend good schools. I can barely manage to put food on the table. Beyond that, there is very little I can do for them.” she said. “When I see my children sitting at home, unable to continue their studies, I can’t sleep, day or night. Financially, I feel completely helpless.”

‘The rising prices are making everything unaffordable’

Balendra Singh is a security guard in India’s national capital, New Delhi. The sixty-seven-year-old lives in a small room in Noida, a city adjacent to New Delhi, with six of his family members. After the US-Israeli war on Iran broke out, he had to send some family back to his village in Lucknow to curtail expensive city life. Lucknow is the capital of Uttar Pradesh state, in which Noida is too.

“I cannot afford to feed so many mouths in a big city today. The inflation has gotten the better of us,” Singh said. “The rising prices are making everything unaffordable – and our salaries stay the same.”

Singh explains how it’s not about what they are putting on the table to eat, but it’s how many people are eating in an expensive city like Noida.

Singh doesn’t own a vehicle, but feels the pinch of rising fuel prices in the extra cost of the rickshaw rides he needs to commute to work.

“The base prices of rickshaws have risen. Even if that rise is five rupees, it is really big for us – because in a month, that’s like 300 rupees ($3) increase for to-and-fro travel to work,” he says, before describing how he and the remaining members of his family in Noida are adapting to the higher cost of living. “We may eat fish once a week rather than thrice a week and put fewer onions in the gravy.”

Singh says when the LNG supply was disrupted earlier in the war, he and his neighbours started using old wood-based fuels. He says he knows the smoke is harmful to health but they had no option — all because of a war that he says he and his country have nothing to do with.

“My children did not attack Iran. My children do not support this war. But we are left here to bear the burden of faraway politics. I want to appeal to the government to take measures to insulate us from the rising prices.”

Asma Begum is a housewife, mother of two and works as a domestic worker in Bangladesh’s capital, Dhaka.

She works in one household, washing dishes and doing other domestic chores, earning around 5,000 taka a month ($41). She would like to earn more, but there appears to be less domestic work available.

“Rich people are also under financial pressure,” she said. “They are trying to manage the household work themselves without keeping domestic help.”

For Asma, that illustrates how the cost-of-living pressure is spreading from one household to another: families facing higher expenses cut discretionary spending, including paid domestic help, which in turn reduces the income opportunities available to lower-income workers like her.

“Everyone has the same problem,” she adds. “We all survive by working.”

Asma says that the strain is not limited to her household. Her parents live in the southern coastal district of Barishal. Her father and brother work as construction workers in the same neighbourhood, while her mother cooks at a mess, despite suffering from cancer.

‘The cost of everything has gone up in recent months’

Gyanu Basent works as a porter in the Gaushala area of Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu. Aged 58, he is the father of a 15-year-old and has his ageing father and siblings as dependents too.

Basent never went to school and had to move to Kathmandu to find work.

“We used to do farming before, but monkeys won’t let us do agriculture. Also, a local cooperative in the village embezzled my father’s life savings,” he said.

“I mostly work as a porter these days. I carry all kinds of loads and these days I am mostly carrying LPG gas [cylinders],” adding that he does not have consistent work.

“I earn around 500 (taka) per day ($4) and there is no set earning. When there is little work, I hardly make 200-300,” says Basent.

He eats in budget-friendly restaurants rather than cooking himself because the cost of essentials has soared in recent months.

“I haven’t been able to send much to my family. Luckily for me, a nonprofit is paying for my daughter’s education. My father manages his money from his elderly allowance,” he said. “I use whatever I save to buy clothes, gifts for my daughter and help my family however I can.”

Reporting from Noida, India, by Yashraj Sharma; from Dhaka, Bangladesh, by Moudud Sajan and from Kathmandu, Nepal, by Samik Kharel

articles.title: Oasis not headlining Glastonbury 2027, organiser Emily Eavis confirms
articles.summary: The rock band will not be stopping at Worthy Farm despite being on tour at that time next summer.
articles.body:
Oasis may be back on tour next summer but they will not be playing Glastonbury Festival, according to co-organiser Emily Eavis.

The band announced a series of 2027 gigs across the UK, Ireland, Europe and the US last week, leaving a potentially Glastonbury-shaped hole in their calendar.

Oasis are due to play concerts at Manchester City's Etihad Stadium on the Friday and Saturday of Glastonbury, but don't currently have their own gig scheduled on the Sunday.

This led some fans to conclude the Gallaghers may have been planning to rock up at Worthy Farm's Pyramid Stage to close the event. But Eavis has put those rumours to bed in a direct response to one Glastonbury-goer on social media.

"Please say you've got Oasis," commented one GlastoFest follower on Instagram .

Eavis replied: "Sorry Jimmy, not this time!"

This tallies with what frontman Liam Gallagher posted on X last month, in response to one fan-site noting they were bookmakers' favourites to headline the festival.

"It's not happening," he wrote. "So all you croc wearing flag waving [people] can calm [...] down."

The band's 38-date tour marks the next phase of their comeback following their acclaimed 2025 live reunion, which made an estimated £300 million.

"Come see. It will not be televised," they announced ahead of the last tour.

It was, however, ultimately documented in their own concert film titled Don't Look Back in Anger, released earlier this month.

The UK's biggest festival, Glastonbury - which is broadcast on the BBC - offers worldwide exposure for artists, but Eavis has been open in the past about paying headliners far less than they'd get elsewhere.

Also, the Gallagher brothers, now both in their 50s, did not play three nights in a row throughout their comeback tour - making the prospect of Glastonbury seem even less likely.

Oasis made their Glastonbury debut in 1994 as cool young things on the NME Stage, now called the Woodsies Stage, before the release of their debut album Definitely Maybe.

They returned to headline the Pyramid Stage the following year, with Take That-turned-solo star Robbie Williams joining them on stage, and again in 2004.

Both Gallaghers performed at Worthy Farm as solo acts during their years apart but it seems they will not return there together, in 2027 at least.

Glastonbury tickets will go on sale on 1 October, though the lineup is not expected to be revealed until the spring.

Last year's Glastonbury Festival saw headline performances from The 1975, Neil Young and Olivia Rodrigo, with Rod Stewart in the so-called legend slot.

Oasis had been among the favourites to headline next year, alongside the likes of the perennially rumoured Taylor Swift and Madonna, as well as Harry Styles, Sam Fender, Ed Sheeran, Sabrina Carpenter and Fred Again.

Previous headliners Radiohead, Pulp and Florence and the Machine have also been mentioned in some quarters along with Rihanna, Lady Gaga, Chappell Roan and Eminem.

Bookies have also provided odds for possible headline sets from Charli XCX, Raye, Bad Bunny, Adele, Miley Cyrus, Kendrick Lamar, Justin Bieber, Bruce Springsteen and Little Simz.

Last month, Eavis confirmed they had booked their headliners for next summer but scotched rumours that Madonna will be among them.

Speaking to Katie Razzall on BBC Radio 4's PM programme, Eavis said: "No, it's definitely not Madonna, I'll tell you that."

She added: "But we have got three [other] headliners and we're very excited about it - it's all coming together really well."

Swift was announced as a headliner for Glastonbury's 50th anniversary in 2020. But that year's festival was cancelled entirely due to the Covid-19 pandemic. So, like Madonna, she is yet to make her Worthy Farm debut.

When asked about the possibility of a performance from Swift at last, Eavis laughed and said she didn't want to discuss the line-up any more.

We'll put her down as a definitely maybe then, for now.

articles.title: United Nations says US may have committed war crimes in Iran: What it means
articles.summary: UN probe finds US unlawfully struck an Iranian school and sports centre, killing children; White House rejects findings.
articles.body:
A United Nations-mandated fact-finding mission has concluded that the United States may have committed war crimes when it carried out two strikes on Iran in February 2026 – one on a primary school in Minab, the other on a sports complex in Lamerd.

The Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on the Islamic Republic of Iran submitted its findings to the UN Human Rights Council after months of investigation into the February strikes, when the US and Israel began the war on Iran amid stalled nuclear negotiations. It concluded that there were reasonable grounds to believe the US acted “recklessly” in the strikes.

Neither Washington nor Israel granted the mission access to personnel or responded to its requests for information, so investigators relied, instead, on satellite imagery, verified video, weapons analysis and witness accounts from Iranian sources and independent organisations.

“The Mission concluded that when identifying and directing its attack against the primary school in Minab, whose civilian nature is apparent, the US failed in its obligation to do everything feasible to verify that it was a military objective,” the report stated.

On February 28, during the opening hours of the joint US-Israeli assault on Iran, missiles hit the Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in Minab, Hormozgan province in southern Iran, at about 10:30am local time (07:00 GMT).

The school was roughly 72 metres from an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) naval facility but was separated from it by a wall, had its own entrance, and was visible in satellite imagery as a functioning school, with children’s murals, a playground and classrooms.

Investigators found that the school had been struck twice. The first strike hit the lower floor; as staff moved children to a prayer room upstairs, a second hit the upper floor, killing many of them.

Local officials put the death toll at 156, including 120 schoolchildren and 26 female teachers. Independent sources cited by the UN mission put the toll at 157, including 15 children aged six.

While the Trump administration initially tried to place the blame on Iranian forces , weapons analysts identified a missile used in the strike as a US Tomahawk Land Attack Missile, which Iran does not possess, from fragments at the site.

At about 5:10pm (13:40 GMT) on February 28, the same day as the Minab strike, there was an air strike on the Shahid Haj Khalil Naimi Cultural and Sports Complex in Lamerd, Fars province – also in the south of the country – a facility the UN-mandated mission said had no military use.

Verified video showed one missile exploding over a nearby residential area, then a second directly above the centre. Local officials reported 22 deaths, including four children, and more than 100 injuries. An adjacent school was also damaged.

What has the US said about these strikes?

Since evidence emerged of the Tomahawk missile at the site of the Minab school strike, the US has not disputed responsibility.

On May 19, CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper said preliminary Pentagon findings “correlated” the strike with US forces. In June, US President Donald Trump said that “nobody” purposefully attacked the school.

The mission also cited reporting by The New York Times and Reuters revealing that a preliminary Pentagon investigation attributed the strike to outdated intelligence that had wrongly identified the school as part of the adjacent military site.

Washington, however, does dispute responsibility for the Lamerd strike.

CENTCOM has claimed the damage is consistent with an Iranian Hoveyzeh cruise missile.

However, the mission rejected that finding, citing weapons experts who identified design differences ruling out the use of a Hoveyzeh and pointing, instead, to a US-made Precision Strike Missile, a weapon the US has publicly confirmed using in Iran for the first time.

What is the White House saying about the UN mission report?

The Trump administration disputes its findings.

White House Deputy Press Secretary Anna Kelly told Al Jazeera: “The UN Human Rights Council has accomplished nothing for human rights, spouting unserious nonsense for decades.”

“The only party in this conflict that has committed war crimes is the Iranian regime, which has murdered thousands of its own people, killed Americans overseas, executed acts of terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz, and launched indiscriminate attacks against its neighbours in the region,” she added.

“The president is courageously ensuring that such an evil country never possesses a nuclear weapon, which will make the entire world safer and more stable.”

Iran has publicly rejected the US denials of the Lamerd strike, insisting the missile responsible was American, not Iranian, and has cited the strikes on Minab and Lamerd as evidence of what it calls indiscriminate attacks by Washington against civilians.

Iranian officials, including Minab Prosecutor Ebrahim Taheri and the Lamerd County Sports and Youth Department, have published their own casualty figures for both sites, putting the Minab toll at 156 and the Lamerd toll at 22.

Iran has previously accused the US and Israel of committing crimes against humanity throughout the war, and has called for international accountability over the strikes.

What does ‘war crime’ mean here, legally?

International humanitarian law requires parties to distinguish military from civilian targets and take “all feasible” precautions before launching strikes.

Reed Brody, a human rights lawyer and member of the International Commission of Jurists, told Al Jazeera that not every violation of the laws of war meets the threshold for a war crime, however.

“For any crime, there has to be an intent element,” he said, adding that no one is alleging the US intended to hit a girls’ school. The relevant standard, he said, is recklessness. Recklessness means acting with awareness of a substantial risk of an unlawful outcome and proceeding regardless. The mission’s report describes this as acting with “dolus eventualis”, a mental state that, under international humanitarian law, is legally sufficient to establish the specific war crime of launching an indiscriminate attack.

Brody said the mission’s “recklessness” finding rests on three factors: outdated targeting data, a building “readily identifiable” as a school, and a US administration he said had made “a practice of weakening and dismantling the systems intended to minimise collateral damage”.

He cited cuts to the Pentagon’s civilian harm mitigation office and remarks by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth favouring “maximum lethality, not tepid legality over stupid rules of engagement”.

The mission concluded the US acted “willfully” with “the requisite mental element of recklessness”, and that its failure to update targeting information “went beyond mere negligence”.

Both incidents could meet the legal threshold for the war crime of launching an indiscriminate attack.

Brody said the US has, at minimum, committed an “internationally wrongful act” by striking civilian sites, drawing a comparison with Nicaragua’s 1980s case against the US over the mining of its harbours after which Washington withdrew its acceptance of the ICJ’s general jurisdiction.

Will there be any consequences for the US?

Brody said the report carries no automatic legal consequences.

“It doesn’t by itself generate any consequences,” he said, adding that such findings can nonetheless “form the basis for other proceedings”, as UN reports have in The Gambia’s genocide case against Myanmar and South Africa’s case against Israel at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague.

However, the US has withdrawn from the ICJ and, Brody said, Iran is unlikely to join the International Criminal Court (ICC), which pursues cases against individuals rather than countries, since doing so would expose its own record to scrutiny.

Brody said accountability ultimately depends on political will rather than legal mechanics. “It means what people make of it,” he said, noting Congress has grown more willing to press the administration as midterm elections approach, which could increase demands for the Pentagon’s internal findings to be made public. “It gives them a hook,” he said – not a binding legal tool, but “more ammunition”.

The UN-mandated mission urged an immediate end to US-Iran hostilities, calling for victim reparations and diplomatic paths towards lasting peace.
