articles.title: There is a way to fix Social Security. And the solution might surprise you
articles.summary: Three proposals to fix Social Security pull every lever: raising the wage cap, a gradual payroll tax increase and pushing full retirement age to 70.
articles.body: Every few months, another headline tells Americans that Social Security is going broke. It's scary. It's also not quite true. Social Security isn't going to wake up one morning with zero dollars coming through the door. Even if its trust fund reserves are depleted, millions of workers will still be paying Social Security taxes every payday. CONGRESS SPENDS $7 TRILLION. HERE’S HOW THAT MATH WORKS OUT IF YOU THINK OF JUST $100 The problem is that those taxes eventually won't generate enough money to pay 100% of scheduled benefits. So, let's stop pretending Social Security can't be fixed. It can. You're just probably not going to like the fix. Here are three changes Washington should seriously consider. 1. Raise the Social Security wage cap to $400,000 In 2026, employees pay 6.2% into Social Security, and employers contribute another 6.2%, but the tax stops once wages reach $184,500. SIX DIFFERENT WAYS THAT PROVE THE WEALTHY PAY A LOT MORE THAN THEIR ‘FAIR SHARE’ Someone making $100,000 pays Social Security tax on every dollar. Someone making $1 million doesn't. That's going to become increasingly difficult politically and mathematically to defend. My first suggestion: Raise the Social Security taxable wage ceiling to $400,000. For somebody earning $400,000, that would expose another $215,500 of wages to Social Security taxes. It also doesn’t make Social Security an infinite tax like Medicare. PROGRESSIVES WANT TO TAX BILLIONAIRES FIRST, AND YOU'RE NEXT ON THE LIST At today's 12.4% combined employee-employer rate, that's potentially another $26,722 annually flowing into the system from that worker and employer combined. Depending on exactly how Congress structured the change, we're potentially talking about well over $1 trillion of additional revenue over a decade. Higher earners won't like it. I wouldn't like paying it either. But Social Security needs revenue. It’s called a compromise. 2. Take the 6.2% tax to 7.2%, one-tenth at a time Here's the second part politicians really won't want to advertise. Especially Democrats. TOP SENATE DEM’S NEW TAX IDEA GETS TORCHED AS CRITICS WARN NEARLY EVERY AMERICAN COULD PAY Everyone needs some skin in the game. Instead of suddenly slamming workers with a giant payroll-tax increase, raise the employee Social Security tax rate from 6.2% to 7.2% gradually over 10 years. That's just 0.1 percentage point each year. Employers would see a corresponding gradual increase. DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS HAVE LOTS OF IDEAS, BUT HOW ARE WE SUPPOSED TO PAY FOR THEM? For someone earning $75,000, the first increase amounts to about $75 for the entire year. Ten years later, the employee would be paying an additional $750 annually at today's income. Higher earners won't like it. I wouldn't like paying it either. But Social Security needs revenue. It’s called a compromise. Nobody enjoys paying more taxes. But slowly adjusting the rate over a decade gives workers and businesses time to adapt. AMERICA'S LIFESPAN HAS DOUBLED SINCE 1776 — EXPERTS REVEAL WHAT CHANGED 3. If you were born after 1990, 70 becomes the new 67 Now comes the third rail. Retirement age. Today's full retirement age is 67 for people born in 1960 or later. Don't change the deal for someone who's 62 and has spent their entire working life planning around 67. Instead, draw a line. If you were born after 1990, gradually move full retirement age to 70. Someone born in 1991 turns 35 this year. They have decades to plan for the change. People are living longer than generations before them. If we're going to make Social Security financially sustainable for another generation, the retirement-age math eventually has to reflect longevity. In the end, nobody gets a free lunch Here's the political problem. Republicans don't want tax increases. Democrats don't want benefit reductions. Workers don't want to pay more. Employers don't want to pay more. High earners certainly don't want another $200,000-plus of wages subjected to payroll taxes. And nobody wants to hear they're working until 70. Welcome to compromise. There are really only three levers available to fix Social Security, and it’s really this simple unless you start doing means testing. Tax more income. Raise more revenue. Reduce future benefits. This plan pulls all three. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Higher earners pay Social Security tax on more wages. Workers and employers gradually contribute more. Younger Americans wait longer for full retirement benefits. And importantly, Social Security doesn't "run out of money." Payroll taxes continue coming in even if the trust fund reserves are exhausted. That's why Congress should stop scaring Americans and start solving the problem. Because the longer Washington waits, the uglier the eventual solution becomes. Nobody gets everything they want under this plan. articles.title: Indonesia gets its first aircraft carrier, sparks debate over cost & military ambitions
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Indonesia on Friday welcomed its first aircraft carrier, a 41-year-old former Italian Navy vessel, as president Prabowo Subianto’s government seeks to.
articles.body: Indonesia on Friday welcomed its first aircraft carrier, a 41-year-old former Italian Navy vessel, as president Prabowo Subianto’s government seeks to modernise the country’s ageing military while positioning the ship as a platform for disaster response.The former ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi arrived at North Jakarta’s Tanjung Priok port after sailing from Italy via the Suez Canal, Red Sea, Colombo and the Malacca Strait. It was received with a military ceremony. The carrier will be renamed the KRI Sriwijaya next week KRI Sriwijaya.Indonesian Navy Chief of Staff Muhammad Ali said the ship would be particularly useful in an archipelago frequently hit by natural disasters.“There are many disasters in this country. So we really need a vessel or platform that could carry many helicopters, because the helicopters can drop logistics quickly to remote areas,” Ali said.“Its condition is still very good and hopefully it can be used by the Indonesian Navy for the next 15 to 20 years.”The 180-metre vessel can carry helicopters and short-takeoff, vertical-landing aircraft and accommodate hundreds of personnel. President Prabowo has said Indonesia plans to refurbish it for helicopter and drone operations rather than use it primarily as a conventional carrier for fighter jets.“We will refurbish it and convert it into a carrier for helicopters and drones,” Prabowo said earlier this month. “This will greatly help our disaster response.”The acquisition has nevertheless prompted questions over cost, operational requirements and Indonesia’s broader military ambitions. The finance ministry approved $450 million in financing for the carrier programme in 2025, while lawmaker TB Hasanuddin said retrofitting alone could cost about 16 trillion rupiah ($900 million).Muhammad Fauzan Malufti of the Center for Strategic and International Studies said the acquisition should be based on operational needs and Indonesia’s ability to sustain the vessel.“The bottom line is that this should not be forced. Otherwise, the benefits could be outweighed by the costs,” Fauzan said.The carrier is expected to undergo refurbishment and integration with Indonesian naval aviation assets.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: The Pentagon is considering a drastic plan to reduce the U.S. military’s presence in Europe. A former detainee at Florida’s “Alligator Alcatraz” detention center said he spent 15 hours in a phone booth-sized cage. Plus, a look at the business of styling tunnel fits for NFL players. Here’s what to know today. Pentagon weighs pulling nearly a third of U.S. forces from Europe The Pentagon is considering a drastic plan to pull planes, ships, weapons and tens of thousands of U.S. troops from Europe, despite warnings from NATO allies about the growing threat of Russian aggression, according to seven current and former U.S. and Western officials. The reduction could be roughly one-third of all U.S. troops in Europe, or about 25,000 — or it could be even larger, as much as half, or up to 40,000 troops. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. If carried out, it would be the most significant scaling back of the 80,000-strong U.S. military presence in Europe since the aftermath of the Cold War in the 1990s. Such a withdrawal could radically reshape America’s relationship with its major allies. Countries affected would likely include Germany, Italy and Spain, sources said. The three nations host the bulk of the U.S. troops in Europe, but leaders of all the countries have also clashed with President Donald Trump over the war with Iran. The Pentagon announced a six-month review of the American military’s presence in Europe in June. Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, the supreme allied commander and the head of the U.S. European Command, is expected to provide his analysis to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth today, sources said. The analysis will likely include four courses of action that could include cuts and possibly shifting some forces within Europe to countries on NATO’s eastern flank. Why some U.S. officials are skeptical of the potential cuts. ‘Godfather of AI’ says there’s little time left to regulate the tech How long does Congress have to implement AI safeguards before it’s too late? “Maybe a year, but not much more than a year,” according to Geoffrey Hinton, a Nobel laureate known as the “Godfather of AI.” Hinton and other experts spoke to lawmakers in a private briefing this week, capping a flurry of activity on Capitol Hill in the week since an Anthropic researcher resigned from his job and warned people of the threat AI poses to humanity. Hinton’s dire warning came as the House departed Washington for the last time before the midterm elections, and there appeared to be lots of conversations but little sign of progress on any substantial AI regulation in the Senate. How lawmakers reacted to Hinton’s warnings. Meanwhile, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro is pushing the federal government to quickly pass regulations to rein in the industry, saying the warnings from tech executives is “not the time to kick the can down the road.” More politics news: Marco Rubio, the nation’s top diplomat, has avoided the spotlight on the unpopular Iran war, distance that could be politically advantageous. Those close to him say a future presidential run or a stint in the private sector could be on the table. For subscribers: Trump administration officials have had discussions with potential replacements for Steve Feinberg, the Defense Department’s No. 2. Former Sen. John Kyl, a longtime Republican lawmaker from Arizona, died at age 84. Former ‘Alligator Alcatraz’ detainee describes phone booth-sized cage For around 15 hours, immigration detention officers at Florida’s “Alligator Alcatraz” kept Raúl Suárez Herrero confined in a cage slightly larger than a phone booth, where he feared snakes and endured mosquitoes in the middle of Florida swampland, he alleged. “I feel like I was in hell,” Suárez said in a phone interview from Mexico, where he was deported. He had lived in the U.S. for more than four decades before he was detained last year during an ICE check-in. Suárez spoke about his experience days after the Department of Homeland Security watchdog confirmed the use of cages — which measured 7 feet, 9 inches high and 4 feet, three inches square — at the now-shuttered detention camp in the Everglades. The facility staff told federal inspectors that the cages were “calming areas” and that no one spent more than two hours inside them. But Suárez said that wasn’t the case. Find out more details from the watchdog report. Related coverage: The White House withdrew Trump’s nominee to lead ICE, former Oklahoma state trooper Lance Schroyer. King Charles issues fiery response to Princess Diana’s brother over claims in new book Buckingham Palace has issued a rare and unusually forceful denial after the late Princess Diana’s brother claimed that the then-Prince Charles said his first wife would soon be forgotten in the days after her death. In a soon-to-be-published memoir, Charles Spencer recounts the emotional days in the aftermath of Diana’s 1997 death in a Paris car crash at age 36. An excerpt alleges a heated exchange with Charles, now the British king, over whether Princes William and Harry — then 15 and 12 — should walk behind their mother’s coffin in the funeral procession. Spencer says he expressed that Diana would not want them to endure such an ordeal and claims that was met with a “stream of anger” from Charles. He writes that Charles “unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. ‘Rest assured,’ he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough.’” Buckingham Palace replied with a forceful statement denying the claims and suggesting that grief for his older sister may have affected Spencer’s memory. “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss,” said the statement. So if they want to show off their individuality, it must be done before they take the field — in the stadium tunnel. Players get off the team bus and walk to the locker room with sharp outfits of all textures and colors. Dallas Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott, for example, stunned last Sunday with a perfectly tailored navy blue suit with baby blue stripes. So how do players decide what to wear each Sunday? articles.title: Wiltshire teens discuss hopes and fears at climate change event
articles.summary: Young people attending a climate change event describe their feelings about the environment.
articles.body:
Teenagers have expressed a mix of worry and optimism about the future of the environment at a conference about sustainability.

Sixth formers from two Wiltshire schools have explained how they feel while at an event for young people discussing sustainable solutions and the future.

Anna said it is a "very big worry" and "quite frustrating because it just feels like not enough action is being taken" while Jed said young people "have a responsibility as the new generation".

They were attending Sustain Britain Schools Conference 2026, started by Sustain Britain after it realised last year it did not have anybody under 35 attending their usual event.

Under-fire ambulance service improves in ratings

Jed, from Royal Wootton Bassett Academy, added that "in the future we are the people that uphold the environment and we may have picked up some bad habits from the people that we've got it from".

"If we started with this after World War Two it would make everyone's lives a lot easier but I think if we need to start getting serious about it, now is the best time.

"And I think we have a chance to make real difference."

Anna, from Malmesbury School, feels education is the most important part.

"I think motivating people and showing the impacts they can have so that they realise how it can affect people and they can try to help."

Fellow Malmesbury pupil Amelia said: "The bad in the news overpowers the good so a lot of people are losing hope in the future for the environment which causes a lot of people to not put in as much as they should to help it, which is why I'm a bit worried about it."

Izzy said she thinks people need to see the "harsh reality of it to have a change".

The conference introduced them to some possible solutions through speakers from lots of different projects - something Emma was pleased about because it made her feel more "confident" that things are going in the right direction.

Ariq feels there is optimism with "upcoming technology" and that "little changes to our lifestyle" can make a big difference.

Thomas said he sees a "a lot of hope still" due to technology and feels there is opportunity to improve how we get energy and "go about our daily lives".

Malmesbury School geography teacher Sarah Blackburn explained that she would be taking some of what was said in the conference back to her lessons, which already include climate change.

"I think it is a lot more shocking to them today than it is when we tell them because they're used to us telling them things, but when they hear it in a different context I think sometimes it sinks in a bit more," said Blackburn.

Nick Ash, from organisers Sustain Britain, wanted to make sure the organisation engaged young people.

"I think in the end, the Sustain project is going to outlast my career by some length.

"We've got to recruit some younger people and get them to carry it forward."

articles.title: NEET paper leak row: SC judges to visit NTA office to inspect upgraded facilities
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Friday highlighted the need to institutionally strengthen the examination system to prevent recurring NEET paper leaks.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Friday highlighted the need to institutionally strengthen the examination system to prevent recurring NEET paper leaks and indicated that judges of the bench would personally visit the National Testing Agency (NTA) to examine its upgraded facilities.Justice Narasimha said the judges would visit the NTA office on Minto Road in Delhi to assess whether the system is functional and examine its manpower and other arrangements.Justice PS Narasimha told Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Centre, that he and Justice Aradhe would like to visit the National Testing Agency's newly upgraded facility to examine its systems.“Strengthening the NTA's system institutionally is crucial to preventing recurring paper leaks. Merely immediate or temporary measures would not suffice. You must know that permanency of the entire system is key. There should be a permanent setup, permanent staff, permanent verticals. Very less deputation should be there. Only then a permanent structure will come up,” the bench told Mehta.At the outset, the Centre told the bench that the high-powered panel led by Nandan Nilekani, constituted to suggest structural reforms in NEET, has held extensive consultations and is likely to submit its first interim report by the end of this month.Solicitor General Tushar Mehta said suggestions received from stakeholders had been placed before the panel, which also held consultations with members of an earlier committee headed by former ISRO chairman K Radhakrishnan.The bench directed the joint secretary of the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT), who is assisting the Nilekani panel, to file an affidavit detailing the steps taken so far.The bench told Mehta that the key issue was to institutionalise the entire process for conducting the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET).The Education Department has said that a new and upgraded system has been created.The bench noted that the Radhakrishnan committee had also recommended structural reforms, but said the key issue was their implementation.Mehta assured the bench that the Nilekani panel was examining all recommendations made by the Radhakrishnan committee, as well as suggestions from the petitioners and other stakeholders.“It is the top most priority of the government. All necessary assistance will be provided,” Mehta told the bench, as cited by PTI.The bench directed that the affidavit filed by the NTA be uploaded on its website to enable people to submit their suggestions.It also asked the Centre to appoint a nodal counsel through whom people could submit their suggestions.On August 19, the Supreme Court, observing the need to institutionalise reforms in the NTA, had directed the Centre to inform it about the steps taken to implement the recommendations of the Radhakrishnan panel and the Nilekani committee.The seven-member Radhakrishnan Committee was constituted by the Ministry of Education following the NEET-UG 2024 paper leak to recommend reforms in the examination process, strengthen data security protocols, and review the structure and functioning of the NTA.Following student protests in July this year, the Union government constituted a high-powered task force headed by Infosys co-founder Nandan Nilekani to suggest structural reforms in competitive examinations.The NTA on May 12 cancelled the NEET-UG 2026 examination held on May 3 following allegations of a paper leak. The matter is being investigated by the Central Bureau of Investigation.A re-test was conducted on June 21, with the results announced on July 16.Following allegations of a NEET-UG question paper leak in 2024, the Supreme Court had declined to cancel the examination but issued several directions to prevent paper leaks and laid down criteria for cancelling public examinations.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Tejas & HTT-40 trainers, Dhruv choppers take flight: HAL's big push to build India's aerospace power
articles.summary: News News: Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) marked a significant milestone in India's aerospace journey by handing over Tejas Final Operational Clearance (FOC.
articles.body: Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) marked a significant milestone in India's aerospace journey by handing over Tejas Final Operational Clearance (FOC) twin-seater trainers and HTT-40 basic trainer aircraft to the Indian Air Force, along with Dhruv Next Generation helicopters to Pawan Hans Limited, at a ceremony in Bengaluru.The defence ministry described the occasion as an important milestone in India's self-reliance journey, showcasing HAL's growing ability, along with its industry partners, to design, develop and manufacture advanced platforms for both military and civil applications.The presence of the HTT-40 alongside Tejas twin-seaters is particularly notable, as the two aircraft now occupy different but complementary stages of the IAF's pilot-training pipeline. The HTT-40 will supplement the Swiss-origin Pilatus PC-7 Mk II at the ab-initio, or basic flying, stage, while the Tejas twin-seater will support advanced type-conversion training.The HTT-40 is a fully aerobatic, tandem-seat turboprop trainer equipped with a glass cockpit, modern avionics, hot-refuelling capability and zero-zero ejection seats. These features are aimed at addressing long-standing gaps in the early stages of IAF pilot training.With an initial indigenous content of 56%, expected to rise beyond 60%, the aircraft also represents a step towards reducing India's dependence on imported training platforms. The IAF has ordered 70 HTT-40 aircraft for Rs 6,800 crore. Deliveries are already a year behind schedule. HAL was originally expected to begin handing over the aircraft in September 2025, with all 70 aircraft scheduled to be delivered by March 2029.The HTT-40 is powered by Honeywell's TPE331-12B turboprop engine.The timing of the handover is significant as the broader Tejas Mk1A programme continues to face delivery delays, partly because of the late supply of GE Aerospace's F404-IN20 engines. The IAF's original order for 83 Mk1A aircraft (comprising 73 fighters and 10 twin-seat trainers) was scheduled to begin deliveries in 2024 and be completed by February 2028. That timeline has since slipped considerably.The delays have stemmed from multiple factors, including HAL's inability to integrate some key aircraft systems within the planned timeframe and GE Aerospace's delayed supply of the F404-IN20 engines.HAL has been contracted to deliver 180 Tejas Mk1A aircraft in total. Of these, 27 airframes have been manufactured so far, while GE has supplied only 10 engines, further constraining the pace of deliveries.Beyond the military side, the inclusion of Dhruv NG helicopters for Pawan Hans broadens the significance of the event to civil aviation. It reinforces the government's broader push to expand indigenous aerospace manufacturing across both defence and commercial applications, a dual-track ambition that HAL is increasingly being positioned to deliver.

articles.title: Shaun the Sheep creators say AI will never replace storytelling as new film launches
articles.summary: The Bristol-based institution have released the third feature film in the Shaun the Sheep franchise.
articles.body:
Shaun the Sheep creators say AI will not replace the craft of storytelling as the franchise's latest film arrives in UK cinemas.

Directed by Steve Cox and Matthew Walker, Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom has a Halloween flavour as Shaun has to turn into a mad scientist to save the day.

Speaking ahead of its launch, producer Richard Beek said despite the rise of AI and CGI within the film industry, stop-motion movies are still being made and winning BAFTAs.

"Maybe somewhere down the line there's a tool we use which uses AI but I don't think it would ever replace the storytelling and creation of those stories," he said.

Despite the film having no dialogue, it has a star-studded voice cast, including Dani Dyer, Justin Fletcher, Nina Sosanya, Paul Whitehouse and Roman Kemp.

It will also feature a brand-new remix of Shaun the Sheep's iconic theme tune, Life's A Treat, by British hip-hop duo Rizzle Kicks.

Aardman celebrated its 50th birthday this year , after it was founded by school friends Sir Peter Lord and Sir David Sproxton in 1976.

The Bristol company went on to create Morph, Wallace and Gromit, Shaun the Sheep and Chicken Run, and become the world's most successful stop-motion film.

Shaun first appeared in the Wallace and Gromit film A Close Shave in 1995 and has become one of the studio's biggest stars.

Like all the other animals, he expresses himself through bleats, grunts and hugely dynamic facial expressions - which is part of his global appeal.

Yet executives repeatedly urged Aardman to give him a voice, when the first TV series launched and the first feature film was made in 2015.

Students at Aardman's Academy are also being taught to embrace imperfection in the painstaking art of stop-motion, where every blink, smile and movement is created by hand.

Art director Kitty Clay said a lot of the models are still being used 20 years after they were made.

She said a lot of the props have "a personal touch" too, from her mum's ironing board to her granny's lampshade in the living room.

Co-director Matthew Walker said: "It's been really exciting to explore a Shaun story in a new genre.

"We did sci-fi with Farmageddon and now we're in Halloween horror but without the scares - it's more comedy," he said.

Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom is showing in UK cinemas this week and next.

The film will then be available to watch later on Sky Cinema and NOW TV.

articles.title: Diana’s brother says Charles sounded ‘giddily elated’ after her death
articles.summary: Buckingham Palace remains gripped in drama as excerpts of Princess Diana’s brother’s book continues to be dripped into the public domain, ahead of its official release next week.
articles.body: LONDON — King Charles III is facing more criticism from Princess Diana’s brother, Charles Spencer, with Buckingham Palace bracing for days of revelations from his tell-all memoir. The latest advance excerpt from the book accuses the then-Prince Charles of sounding “giddily elated” and “like a lottery winner,” immediately after Diana’s death in a Paris car crash in 1997, one year after they finalized their divorce. Spencer, an earl whose aristocratic family has generational ties with Britain’s royal family, writes that he was at his home in South Africa with his children when he learned “in the middle of the night” from his sister Jane Fellowes that Diana had been in a car crash. He later learned, “after escalating dread,” that she had died. “The phone rang constantly. Prince Charles caught me as I crossed the landing upstairs,” he wrote. “Unlike my other callers, who were stunned, barely able to articulate their condolences and offers of help, he sounded giddily elated — like a lottery winner, I remember thinking at the time.” On the call, Spencer wrote, Charles told him that he had informed Princes William and Harry, then 15 and 12, of their mother’s death. “Looking back now, I suspect the prince’s first reaction must have been to think more of how this event might free him to marry the woman he loved, rather than appreciating the loss of one he did not. It can be hard to feel too much sympathy for an ex-spouse, or those who care for them profoundly, after bitter divorce,” he added. Spencer also detailed feeling shut out by royal protocol during Diana’s funeral arrangements, alleging that royal officials turned down a request to play music loved by Diana — Mozart’s “Requiem” — during her funeral. “Diana remained theirs, in Buckingham Palace’s eyes, even in death. Her family, despite her divorce, were simply expected to fall into line with any royal decisions,” he added. In the first wave of revelations from the book earlier this week, Spencer alleged that Charles had told him that Diana would soon be forgotten in the days after her death. Buckingham Palace released an unusually forceful statement denying Spencer’s claims and suggesting that grief for his older sister may have impacted his memory. “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss,” the statement said Wednesday. A spokeswoman for Buckingham Palace declined to further comment Friday, telling NBC News that “we do not comment on books as a policy,” and referring to Wednesday’s statement. Spencer’s book, “Swan Song: Diana, My Sister,” is due to be released publicly Tuesday. Britain’s Daily Mail newspaper is publishing excerpts in advance, while an interview with Spencer is due to air on CBS on Sunday. Thursday’s tranche of new excerpts continued to provide difficult reading for the palace, reflecting on the breakdown of Diana and Charles’ marriage. Spencer writes that his sister “told me that things became very difficult indeed in the marriage early on, and I am sure that both spouses despaired of the other at times.” “I am not hypocritical enough to judge or criticise anyone else’s marital record. I am merely recording how my sister felt and am not assessing whether she was right or not,” he added. Spencer also writes about Diana’s struggle with an eating disorder, which she spoke about during her lifetime, as well as her wider mental state, criticizing her transfer from a long-serving family doctor to a royal physician. “It is a sad fact that, in her later years, Diana drove herself more than once to Beachy Head, the highest chalk sea cliff in England, while contemplating ending it all. Her love for her sons stopped her from going further,” he writes. The royal family continued to undertake a busy schedule of public duties this week. Charles made headlines at an event meeting with senior figures in AI at a summit in Scotland, while the Prince and Princess of Wales, William and Kate, attended charitable events there. Prince Harry, who returned to the United Kingdom last month but remains a nonworking member of the royal family, was also photographed for the first time since his return, at a charitable function Thursday. Harry, whose own bombshell memoir “Spare” rattled the royal establishment in 2023, has remained close to the Spencer family, with his own book thanking “my mother’s siblings for their love, support, time, and perspective.” He did not respond to questions shouted by reporters about his uncle’s book Thursday. If you or someone you know is struggling or in emotional distress, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org 24/7 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For additional resources, visit SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources. The National Alliance for Eating Disorders Helpline provides support, resources and information about treatment options at 1-866-662-1235, Monday through Friday. You can also text “ALLIANCE” to 741741 if you are experiencing a crisis to be contacted by a trained volunteer. More information about eating disorders, including other free and low-cost support options, can be found on the National Eating Disorder Association’s website.

articles.title: The view from Russia: ‘No party can be antiwar’ in parliamentary election
articles.summary: First vote since Russia invaded Ukraine seen as a sham by some and an opportunity to strengthen nationalism by others.
articles.body:
This weekend, Russians are heading to the ballot box to vote in the first parliamentary election since the war with Ukraine began in early 2022.

Theoretically up for grabs are 450 seats in Russia’s parliament, the Duma, though the governing United Russia party, led by President Vladimir Putin, is expected to retain its comfortable majority.

One of the hopefuls is Damir Gurin, who is running for the Green Party in Russia’s Far Eastern Federal District, where the forests of Siberia meet the Pacific Ocean. His policies include affordable housing, monitoring industrial emissions and promoting recycling over landfills.

“My goal is to provide this harsh land and its people with worthy ecological and institutional representation,” Gurin told Al Jazeera. “We’re not just solving the problems of nature, we’re protecting the human habitat.”

Although the environment is a concern in Russia, other issues may overshadow it.

An advertisement promoting the elections on state-run TV depicting famed Russian warriors through history ends with the words: “Their voice is the voice of victory. Your vote is the strength of Russia!”

“This extensive election campaign is taking place as we continue the special military operation,” Putin stated in a public address on Wednesday, using the official euphemism for the invasion of Ukraine. “Your choice and determination will show once again that millions of people are backing our fighters and that we stand together.”

Among the top candidates being fielded by United Russia are the hawkish former president Dmitry Medvedev and Vladislav Golovin, a veteran of the siege of Mariupol.

Ilya Budraitskis, a Russian social scientist based in California, said the Kremlin is seeking a popular mandate for its handling of the Ukraine war.

“Putin constantly describes [Ukraine President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy as illegitimate, because he does not hold an election in wartime,” Budraitskis told Al Jazeera. “In Russia, as Putin has just stressed, in strict accordance with the schedule, as per the law, elections are held on time, and, accordingly, the Russian authorities keep their legitimacy.”

The elections come as the war is being increasingly felt on the home front.

On Friday morning, Ukraine launched more than 350 drones towards Moscow as the election got under way.

Kyiv’s attacks on Russian oil infrastructure have caused fuel shortages, while the authorities have imposed internet blackouts in the name of national security.

“If there’s fuel at the gas station, people immediately line up,” said Aleksey, a Saint Petersburg resident in his mid-thirties who declined to provide his full name.

“My mother lives outside the city near a gunpowder factory, and [drone attacks] happen periodically,” he said. There are “loud explosions, the ceiling shakes and plaster falls off the house, and sometimes she has to hide in the bathroom with the dog”.

According to the independent pollster Levada, more than half of Russians support peace talks, yet nearly 70 percent say they also support the actions of the armed forces in Ukraine.

“I spent a week in my home village, and in the past year the mood there has gotten so bad in terms of radicalisation, militarisation, human rights, and so on,” said Katherine, a St Petersburg psychiatrist in her sixties, who requested Al Jazeera withhold her surname.

“Bombing everyone, taking everything away from all the ‘damned traitors’… I don’t know if my neighbours can be considered a focus group, but if so, the prospects don’t look very encouraging.”

Exiled opposition figures based abroad, including Ilya Yashin and Yulia Navalnaya , have urged Russians to vote for any party other than United Russia.

Max, a young Muscovite, said he has used an online tool which advises dissenting Russians who to vote for.

“They tell me which candidate, not from the ruling party, has the best chance of winning. This won’t lead to an end to the war, but at least I can sleep soundly,” he told Al Jazeera.

Aleksey is considering voting for the Communist Party “even though I understand that in the current situation, no party can be against war”.

Of all of Russia’s major parties, only the liberal Yabloko openly opposes the war and calls for an immediate ceasefire.

But in August, a judge excluded it from the election after a complaint from a small nationalist party, Rodina, over alleged copyright infringement, “extremism”, and overseas funding.

“Of course, it happened because according to polls, Yabloko would have overcome the 5 percent barrier,” the minimum seats needed to win Duma representation, said Budraitskis.

“Yabloko would have led an election campaign under these slogans of immediate peaceful negotiations, the lifting of all [wartime] restrictions, the cessation of repression, and so on. And it would be extremely dangerous to allow such a public campaign, because it was obviously popular.”

But for Sergey Kalenik, a Moscow-based media professional who supports Putin’s government, the exclusion of Yabloko means Russian democracy has “flourished.”

“Previously, elections were a real life-or-death struggle, because any attempts by patriots to gain ground were blocked,” he told Al Jazeera.

He described Yabloko cofounder Grigory Yavlinsky as “a fanatical Ukrainian nationalist [who] wants to make all Russians slaves of Ukrainians.”

“What kind of democracy can there be when such a party exists in parliament?” he asked rhetorically.

Nevertheless, although most of their candidates were disqualified, individual Yabloko members are still allowed to run for single-mandate constituencies rather than competing on a party-list basis. In Moscow, Yabloko’s Polina Lermant handed out flyers urging Muscovites to “vote for peace”.

Gurin, the Green candidate, acknowledged that lawsuits and allegations could be political tricks, but said dozens of candidates from other parties have also been disqualified, including Nikolai Bondarenko, the Saratov representative of the normally pro-Kremlin Communists.

“The political environment is an arena of strict discipline and competition,” said Gurin.

articles.title: HAL hands over LCA FOC trainers, first HTT-40 ‘Ankur’ to IAF, 4 Dhruv-NG Choppers to Pawan Hans
articles.summary: Defence News: BENGALURU: Defence PSU HAL Friday handed over two LCA Tejas twin-seater trainers in the final operational clearance (FOC) configuration, and the first.
articles.body: BENGALURU: Defence PSU HAL Friday handed over two LCA Tejas twin-seater trainers in the final operational clearance (FOC) configuration, and the first of the HTT-40 basic trainer to the Indian Air Force (IAF), while also handing over four Dhruv Next Generation (Dhruv-NG) helicopters to Pawan Hans Limited.The LCA trainer delivery completes the twin-seater deliveries under the FOC contract, while the Dhruv-NG and HTT-40, whose name “Ankur” was formally announced Friday, marks the beginning of the deliveries under those respective contracts.Defence minister Rajnath Singh, and civil aviation minister K Rammohan Naidu were present at the handing-over ceremony. The LCA FOC Trainer is a lightweight, all-weather, multi-role aircraft to support IAF’s Tejas training requirements. It can undertake fighter operations when required.“It incorporates contemporary technologies including: relaxed static stability, quadruplex fly-by-wire flight-control system, carefree manoeuvring, advanced glass cockpit, integrated digital avionics and advanced composite materials for the airframe. These have enabled India to develop and operationalise an advanced twin-seat fighter aircraft capability,” HAL said.A contract for 16 LCA fighter aircraft and four FOC Trainers was placed in 2010 by MoD/IAF, a year after Aeronautical Development Agency (ADA) achieved FOC.“In 2022–23, all 16 FOC fighter aircraft were delivered. Sept 2023 saw the release to service (RSD) milestone for the twin-seater. In 2024-25, delivery of FOC trainers began with SPT5 and SPT6, while the final two — SPT7 and SPT8 — were produced. In Nov-Dec 2025, software-defined radio (SDR) was incorporated on the final two,” HAL said.The SPT7 and SPT8 had enhancements of radar, autopilot, fuel-system, avionics software and air-to-air refueling probe. Looking ahead, HAL said it’s focussed on LCA-Mk1A twin-seaters being developed under the 83 and 97-aircraft contract. “While the 83 contract trainers will have enhanced capabilities, those under 97-contract will incorporate capabilities of Mk1A fighter,” HAL said.“The capabilities include AESA (Active Electronically Scanned Array) radar, electronic warfare suite, avionics upgrades, modernised mission and display systems, LDP4i (Litening 4i Laser Designator Pod) integration, IRNSS, HMDAS DASH V (an advanced helmet-mounted display system), additional weapons capabilities, including beyond visual range and advanced short range air-to-air missile,” HAL said, adding that it hopes to deliver 29 Mk1A twin-seaters by 2033–34.HTT-40 ‘Ankur’The HTT-40 handover marks the beginning of deliveries under MoD’s 70-aircraft contract. It is designed for multiple stages of basic pilot training, including basic training, aerobatics, general handling, instrument flying, navigation, night flying and close formation flying.“It is supported by a broader training ecosystem comprising cockpit procedure trainer (CPT), full base fixed mission simulator (FBFMS), computer-based training (CBT), which complement flying training and enable trainees to familiarise themselves with aircraft procedures, systems and mission-related activities,” HAL said.“Ankur, powered by a 1,100 SHP turboprop engine has a maximum speed of 300 knots, normal training weight of 2,960 kg, service ceiling of 6,000 m, range of 1,000km, endurance of around 3 hours with a fuel capacity of 450kg. It has a 11-m wing span, 10.06-m length, 3.5-m height, maximum load factor of +6/-3g, ejection seat and features an air-conditioned cockpit and modern avionics system, supporting the requirements of contemporary military pilot training,” it added.Designed by HAL's Aircraft Research and Design Centre (ARDC), the aircraft can provide good low-speed handling characteristics and effective training for trainee pilots. It completed the first flight on May 31, 2016, underwent an extensive programme of development, evaluation and validation trials with HAL and IAF.“The aircraft has completed trials covering handling qualities, stability and control, systems performance, engine relight, hot-weather operations, sea-level operations, crosswind operations, night flying and range and endurance.Dhruv-NGThe Dhruv-NG is a 5.5-tonne, light twin-engine, multi-role helicopter developed to address demanding operating conditions in India and upgraded for the requirements of the global civil aviation market.“It’s India’s first indigenously produced civil helicopter meeting the AS-4 requirements, making it suitable for offshore operations. The helicopter is equipped with twin Shakti 1H1C engines, and features civil-certified glass cockpit, modern avionics suite, advanced navigation systems and enhanced situational awareness,” HAL said.It added that safety features include crashworthy seats, self-sealing fuel tanks and a twin-engine configuration providing redundancy. “Dhruv NG has a configurable cabin that can be adapted for different civilian roles, including: VIP/VVIP transport (luxury for 4–6 passengers), passenger/utility (up to 14 passengers) air ambulance (four stretchers, a doctor and an attendant), specialised operations, including offshore operations, law enforcement, disaster relief and search & rescue,” HAL said.The PSU is also offering after-sales and lifecycle support. Integrated logistics support will include power-by-hour (PBH) and performance-based logistics (PBL) models for fleet serviceability.

articles.title: Flight chaos caused by software defect, says air traffic control body
articles.summary: The failure led to more than 2,000 flights being cancelled and hundreds of thousands of passengers affected.
articles.body:
An air traffic control system failure that sparked widespread travel chaos earlier this month was caused by a "software defect", the UK's national air traffic service (Nats) has said.

The failure led to more than 2,000 flights being cancelled and hundreds of thousands of passengers affected, with some sleeping on airport floors or getting stuck overseas.

Flights in and out of the UK's main airports were affected, including Heathrow, Gatwick, Luton and Glasgow.

The incident prompted questions over the resilience of Nats' systems, and some airlines questioned the position of its chief executive Martin Rolfe.

There has also been anger from passengers about how much support they got from airlines.

The government had previously ruled out a cyber attack, and last week the Ministry of Defence denied a report that a military aircraft was to blame.

In an initial report, Nats said the defect happened in the system which "underpins the management of UK airspace".

The problem happened "in the space of a millisecond", Nats said, leading to the system producing corrupted data.

Martin Rolfe said: "I would like to apologise again, very sincerely, to everyone who was affected last week.

"It's our job to get people where they want to go, quickly and without delay and we are devastated when that goes wrong.

"However, our primary role is to keep our skies safe, and everyone who flies through them. At no point last week was safety in question."

articles.title: As Houthis grab Bab al-Mandeb, US appears willing to watch from sidelines
articles.summary: Stretched by its war with Iran, Washington may have little choice but to trust Houthi assurances on shipping.
articles.body:
United States officials met Houthi representatives at the US embassy in the Omani capital, Muscat, over the weekend after the Iran-aligned movement seized thousands of square kilometres of territory in just a few days.

With strategically important islands and large stretches of Yemen’s Red Sea coast now under Houthi control, the group has tightened its grip on the Bab al-Mandeb Strait – a crucial chokepoint for global shipping and energy supplies.

During the talks, the Houthis assured US officials that they had no intention of attacking US shipping in the Red Sea, saying their restrictions would apply only to vessels linked to Saudi Arabia.

But that would still leave two of the world’s most important shipping routes facing serious disruption, with traffic through the Strait of Hormuz restricted for the past six months. Any further disruption could drive global oil and consumer prices even higher, creating another political headache for US President Donald Trump ahead of midterm elections in November.

With the Houthis’ history of attacking commercial vessels, their ties to Iran and their deep ideological opposition to the US, some experts question how far their assurances can be trusted. But some analysts say Washington may have little choice but to take the group at its word, at least for now. US military resources are reportedly depleted and growing domestic opposition to the Iran war have all limited Washington’s ability – and willingness – to open another front in Yemen.

As the Houthis seized territory in southwestern Yemen, the US publication Axios reported that Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called Donald Trump twice last week, urging him to launch strikes against the group – but the US president refused.

Admiral Brad Cooper, the commander of US Central Command, subsequently travelled to Riyadh for urgent coordination talks with the crown prince. The visit suggested Washington was seeking to intensify support for Saudi Arabia while avoiding direct military involvement.

Trump also attempted to reassure Riyadh, describing the crown prince as a “good friend” and promising that “everything will work out very well”.

But he offered no specific military commitment and the White House announced no explicit guarantee that the US would defend Saudi energy infrastructure or shipping routes.

Axios also reported that the military chiefs of Israel, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt attended a private gathering convened by the US.

While the US has avoided intervening, Israel, whose ships and territory have previously been targeted by the Houthis, has reportedly offered to intervene in Yemen on Saudi Arabia’s behalf. Simon Mabon, a professor of international relations at Lancaster University, however, said any Israeli involvement would probably be limited.

“With elections coming up [in Israel], there comes a point when there is overreach,” Mabon told Al Jazeera. “In light of Gaza, Lebanon, Syria and the West Bank – as well as the question marks over Iran – Yemen could be a bridge too far.” Experts also say that the Saudis may be wary of being seen to rely on Israeli military support, particularly amid the war on Gaza, because doing so could damage Riyadh’s standing and legitimacy throughout the Arab and Muslim worlds.

Washington’s reluctance to act could deepen Saudi concerns about its longstanding security relationship with the US. “This is another instance of the United States failing to fulfil its role as a security guarantor,” Mabon said. “That will start to add up and create serious doubts in Saudi Arabia about whether it can rely on the United States.”

The kingdom began diversifying its relationships after attacks on its oil infrastructure in 2018 and 2019 exposed the limits of US security guarantees. Last September, it signed a mutual defence agreement with Pakistan, stipulating that an attack on either country would be treated as an attack on both. Riyadh expanded that emerging security arrangement last month by signing the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement with Pakistan and Turkiye, under which an armed attack against any of the three would be regarded as an attack against them all.

Mabon said the latest crisis was unlikely to produce a complete break with Washington, but could accelerate Riyadh’s efforts to build closer ties elsewhere.

“We are already seeing a diversification of security portfolios,” he said. “The Saudis are starting to believe that they cannot rely on the United States all the time, which is why we saw the agreement with Turkey and Pakistan.”

Washington is already embroiled in an expensive and resource-intensive war with Iran, the Houthis’ principal regional backer. Trump entered that conflict expecting it to end within days. More than six months later, the war remains unresolved, oil prices are higher and the administration has yet to set out a clear route towards ending it.

Opening another front in Yemen would risk repeating that experience at a particularly difficult moment for Trump’s Republican Party. A new campaign in Yemen could complicate closely contested House and Senate races, especially after Trump built his presidential campaign around the promise to end US involvement in “forever wars”. A Reuters/Ipsos poll published last month found that just 31 percent of Americans supported US military action against Iran, down from 37 percent in March, while 83 percent expected the conflict to continue for an extended period.

“The elections in November are hugely significant,” Mabon said. “Republicans will be anxious about all of this. Opening a new front in what could potentially become another forever war would be deeply unpopular.”

It is questionable whether the US has the military resources required to sustain another operation. Reports emerged in July that supplies of some critical munitions, particularly long-range missiles and Patriot interceptors, were running low. Those concerns coincided with Washington halting attacks on Iran.

A Pentagon watchdog report published this week found that the first four months of the war cost $33bn, including $22bn in expended munitions. It also revealed that dozens of aircraft had been lost or damaged, hundreds of buildings and structures hit and Iranian attacks caused an estimated $184m in damage to US diplomatic facilities.

The Trump administration has denied that the US is running short of weapons, insisting that it retains “massive amounts” of weaponry.

But about 50 military officers and civilian officials working with the Joint Staff were ordered to take polygraph lie detector tests as the administration sought to identify the source of leaks about military readiness and weapons stocks.

“We know there are hugely depleted weapons stockpiles, which have prompted some US officials to urge a pause in the war on Iran,” Mabon said.

“When you put that together, it is probably the main reason Trump said no to MBS.”

Washington’s response may also reflect the different strategic importance it places on the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb. Hormuz carries oil and gas from Gulf producers to a global market on which the US economy depends. Bab al-Mandeb has become particularly important for trade to Asia and China.

Some analysts have therefore argued that prolonged disruption could hurt Beijing more severely than the US. China remains somewhat dependent on imported energy via the Red Sea. Higher oil prices can also benefit US energy companies, some of which have donated millions of dollars to Trump and the Republican Party.

But Bab al-Mandeb disruption would not fall neatly along geopolitical lines, experts say. Attacks on Saudi infrastructure and shipping would directly harm one of Washington’s closest regional partners, while higher transport and energy costs would eventually feed into prices paid by US consumers.

Mabon rejected the suggestion that Trump was pursuing a calculated strategy of tolerating disruption to weaken China or reward his donors.

“The potential closure of Bab al-Mandeb and strikes on the Saudi pipeline will hit major US allies harder than China,” he said. Whatever benefits higher prices might bring US oil producers would be outweighed politically by the damage inflicted on consumers and the wider economy, he added.

With the US already stretched by war with Iran – which the Trump administration initially expected to end within days – Washington may now be confronting the reality that entering another war in the Middle East carries considerable military, economic and electoral risks.

“I don’t see any kind of grand strategy at play here,” Mabon said. “There is no off-ramp regarding Iran and I think that, in the case of Yemen, there is no easy off-ramp either.”

articles.title: Holdout Lindsay Clancy juror will not be giving interviews, his attorney says
articles.summary: The lone holdout juror in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial will not be giving interviews or speaking out on what happened in the Massachusetts courtroom during the dayslong deliberations before a judge declared a mistrial earlier this month, according to a statement from his lawyer.
articles.body: The lone holdout juror in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial will not be giving interviews or speaking out on what happened in the Massachusetts courtroom during the dayslong deliberations before a judge declared a mistrial earlier this month, according to a statement from his lawyer. “While I appreciate and respect the numerous understandable media requests that have poured in this evening regarding our American Hero and Champion of Justice, he will not be giving any interviews at this time,” the man’s lawyer, Edward Andrew Paltzik, said in a post on X. “None. Zero.” Paltzik added that he “too will not be giving any interviews on his behalf at this time. None. Zero.” As deliberations in the triple murder trial unfolded over a matter of days, it became increasingly clear that the 12-person jury, comprised of nine women and three men, would not reach a unanimous verdict. The foreperson issued deadlock notices to Massachusetts Superior Court Judge William Sullivan twice before returning to the courtroom to say one juror was not following the reasonable doubt standard and was blocking a unanimous decision. Sullivan then sent jurors back to deliberations once more before they again returned with the news that they were deadlocked for a third time, forcing the judge to declare a mistrial Sept. 4. “We are focused entirely on his health, safety, and well-being,” Paltzik said in the statement about his client. “There will be a time for accountability and a time for the real story of the Lindsay Clancy Trial to be told. But not right now.” The jury was tasked with determining whether Clancy was guilty of murdering her three children, Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, by strangling them with exercise bands Jan. 24, 2023. Her defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, argued that she was in psychosis at the time of the killings, a result of the postpartum psychosis she was suffering from. But prosecutors said that Clancy was not in psychosis, that she was aware of her actions at the time and that she had planned the murders ahead of time. Clancy’s then-husband, Patrick Clancy, and his new wife, Dr. Rachel Danis, will be speaking out on the case for the first time Sunday in an appearance on “60 Minutes.” Online sleuths and true-crime fanatics watching the broadcast trial had peddled conspiracy theories that it was actually Patrick Clancy who killed the children and framed Clancy. While the prosecution was gunning for a first-degree murder conviction, the jury could have also convicted Clancy of lesser charges — second-degree murder or manslaughter — or deemed her not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility. At least five other jurors have since spoken out and described hostility and disinterest from the holdout juror, who identified himself to NewsNation as Michael P. Desronvil. Three women on the jury — including the foreperson — told NBC Boston that 11 of the jurors agreed to find Clancy not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility. Desronvil wanted to convict, they revealed, but admitted he expressed doubt in the prosecution’s case. Nick Dargie, one of the three men on the jury, told “Good Morning America” that Desronvil was often disengaged and scrolling on his phone during deliberations. In the interview, Dargie acknowledged that it’s fair for someone to have a differing opinion from the group but said this particular juror would not engage and could not “find something to support his view.” Another female juror who spoke to WBZ-TV of Boston anonymously chalked it up to someone who couldn’t let go of his convictions. But Desronvil told NewsNation that wasn’t true and that he never had doubts. “As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence present,” Desronvil said in the statement. “Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses, and what the prosecution presents, I thought it was enough proof that she (Clancy) knew exactly what she was doing and planned.” Paltzik asked that no one contact Desronvil and that the public “respect his dignity, humanity, and privacy.” “Stay away from his home, stop calling him, and don’t even think about deciphering his location,” Paltzik said in the statement. Paltzik said he and his client “look forward to sharing more information in the coming days on an appropriate timeline.” Prosecutors for the commonwealth of Massachusetts must now decide whether to retry Clancy. Reddington has filed a motion to drop the charges, and the next hearing is scheduled for Sept. 29.
